en: Prosperity!

I bow with my speech to the Lord of Architecture, the elephant-faced one, the son of the non-elephant-born (Pārvatī), the auspicious shatterer of the mountain of obstacles; and to the Goddess of Speech, who possesses the luster of a mandāra flower. (1)
Having prostrated before Viśvakarman, the supreme lord of artisans,
I shall expound the science of architecture (Vāstuvidyā) according to my ability and in brief.
In this regard, I shall first explain the means of measurement for all things, since by means of measurement alone everything in the world is established. (3)
The atom (paramāṇu), when increased sequentially, is known as the measure-finger (mānāṅgula); what is called an atom is within the range of vision of yogins. 4.

Eight atoms (paramāṇu) are known as one mote of dust in a sunbeam (trasareṇu); likewise, from the mote of dust come the hair-tip (romāgra), the nit (likṣā), the louse-egg (yūkā), and the barley-corn (yava).
The eightfold increments are said to be [the units of measurement], and eight times a barley-corn (yava) is a finger-breadth (aṅguli).
A finger-breadth is the measure for a vitasti, which consists of ten finger-breadths.

In the science of architecture (vāstuvidyā), this *hasta* has been specified by you, and it is traditionally known as a *kiṣku*. A measure of twenty-five *aṅgulas* is traditionally known as a *prājāpatya*. Twenty-six [aṅgulas] is a *dhanurmuṣṭi*; twenty-seven [aṅgulas] is a *dhanurbraha*. Twenty-eight *aṅgulas* is a *prācya*; a *vaideha* is nineteen [aṅgulas]. A *vaipulya* is thirty *aṅgulas*, while a *prakīrṇaka* is thirty-one. For vehicles and beds, the *kiṣku* is used; for palaces, the *prājāpatya*.

For sacred sites (*vāstu*), such as villages and the like, the measurement is the *dhanurmuṣṭi*; however, for all sacred sites, it is considered to be the *kiṣku*. It is proclaimed as being to the north of the *jagatī* or according to the birth-measure (*janman*). In the abodes of the gods, the *daṇḍa* is used; among humans, it is four *karas*. Now, I shall briefly describe the individual characteristics of artisans: the master builder (*sthapati*) must be worthy of installation and proficient in all scriptures.

Neither deficient-limbed nor having extra limbs, he is righteous and devoted to compassion; free from envy and malice, he is a master of the Tantras and of noble birth. (13) He is an expert in mathematics and the Purāṇas, joyful in soul and free from greed; he is knowledgeable in the arts, conversant with all lands, truthful, and has conquered his senses. (14) He is healthy and vigilant, devoid of the seven vices; he possesses an auspicious name, has steadfast kinsmen, and has reached the further shore of the ocean of architecture. (15) Chapter One.

The disciple of that master, or his son, who follows the master’s instructions and is skilled in all crafts; who knows the measurements of the cord and the staff, and understands the standards of measurement and weighing—he is called the *vardhaki*. He always follows the *sūtragrāhin* and effects the growth [of the structure] by means of skillful application upon the pieces already hewn. Furthermore, he who hews both the thick and the thin parts is celebrated as the *takṣaka*. || 16–18 ||

One who knows the work of clay, who is virtuous, capable, independent in all tasks, devoted to the Guru, always joyful, and ever following the Sthapati and the others—without these, it is impossible for anyone to perform any rite. Therefore, this group of four, beginning with the Sthapati, is always worthy of worship. Without these—the Sthapati and the others—it is impossible in this world to acquire merit; therefore, mortals who enjoy [the fruits] resort to the Guru together with them, and thus they experience joy.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Means," in the Science of Architecture (*Vāstuvidyā*). Now begins the second chapter. Now, therefore, I shall indeed proclaim the Science of Architecture as it was in the past. First one should examine the ground, and afterwards one should commence the construction of the site (*vāstu*). (1) I shall describe the incline of the earth and its auspicious and inauspicious effects for men. An incline toward the east is known to bring prosperity; an incline toward the north is recorded as bestowing wealth. One should know that an incline toward the west causes the loss of wealth. (2)

The earth sloping toward the south brings death to men. That which is joined with the exaltation of Varuṇa and conjoined with the depression of Indra is to be known as the *Gotrīvīthī*; that which has the exaltation of Indra and the depression of Varuṇa is called the *Jalavīthī* by those expert in the knowledge of Vāstu. That which has the exaltation of Soma and the depression of Yama is called the *Yamavīthī*; and that which has the exaltation of Yama and the depression of Soma is called the *Gajavīthī*. When the exaltation is of Īśa and the depression is of Nirṛti, it is the *Bhūtavīthikā*, the ground of the spirits.
The path of the Nagas is praised as being high for Agni and low for Vayu; that which is high for Vayu and low for Agni, they know as the path of Vaiśvānara.

It is not seen in the two books. Chapter Two. The region between Nirṛti and Īśāna is declared to be the *Dhanavīthī* (Wealth Lane); it is high (*ucca*) for Indra and low (*nīca*) for Varuṇa and Vāyu. One should know this as the *Paitāmaha-vāstu* (Grandfather’s Site); it brings auspiciousness to men. The region between Yama and Agni is high; it is low for Māruta and Soma. That site is named *Supatha* (Good Path); it is praised for all undertakings. The region between Soma and Īśāna is low; it is high for Nirṛti and Kāla.

That dwelling named Dīrghāyu is praised and increases one's lineage; it is situated between Īśāna and Indra, low and high [respectively], and between Varuṇa and Rakṣas. That dwelling named Puṇyaka brings auspiciousness to the twice-born; it is situated between Indra and Agni, low and high [respectively], and between Vāyu and Jaleśa. That dwelling named Apatha leads to enmity and strife; it is situated between Kālāgni and Vāyu, low and high [respectively], and between Vāyu and Soma. That dwelling named Rogakṛt causes the increase of disease for men.

Between Nirṛti and Antaka (Yama) is the low [direction], and between Soma and Śiva is the high; let that site be named Argala, which destroys sins such as the killing of a Brahmin. Between Rudra and Indra is the high [direction], while between Varuṇa and Rakṣas is the low; in the science of architecture, let that site be named Remaśāna, which brings about the total destruction of one's lineage. Between Agni is the low [direction], and between Nirṛti, Īśāna, and Vāyu is the high; let that site be named Śyenaka, which leads to ruin and death. Between Rudra, Abhi, and Varuṇa is the high [direction], and likewise, it would be low in the direction of Nirṛti.

17–20. A site named Śvamukha (Dog’s Face) brings about the fruit of poverty. A site that is high toward Nirṛti, Agni, and Śiva, but low toward Viṣṇu and Indra, is likewise [inauspicious]. A site named Brahmana is always undesirable for living beings. If it were high toward Agni but low toward Nirṛti and Rudra, and if that site were low toward Vāta, it would be called Sthāvara; such a site is auspicious. It should be high in the region of Nirṛti and low toward Jvalana (Agni) and Vāta.

If the depression of the tank is toward Rudra (the north-east), it is called *sthaṇḍila*, which is auspicious; however, if the elevation is toward Rudra while the depression is in the directions of Agni (south-east), Nirṛti (south-west), or Vāyu (north-west), that tank is called *śāṇḍula* and always brings about inauspiciousness. If the elevation is toward Nirṛti, Agni, or Śiva (the north-west) and the depression is toward the Moon (the north) or the Lord of Mountains (the east), [it is likewise unfavorable]. Chapter Two. The earth is declared to be a good site for the best of the twice-born if it is low toward Indra (the east), elevated toward Nirṛti (the south-west), and elevated toward the west and the wind (the north-west).

That which is named Sulabha (Easy-to-Obtain) increases the king and the kingdom; it is exalted in the directions of the Moon, Lord [Ishana], and Wind, and becomes low in the direction of Yama. By name, that which is called Vastuchara grants the desires of Vaishyas; it is low in the direction of Varuna and becomes exalted in the directions of Ishana, Indra, and Agni respectively. That which is named Vaimukha grants the desires of Shudras. Furthermore, that ground which has a gentle slope toward the north, is adorned with Kusha and Darbha grass, and possesses the fragrance of clarified butter, is praised for Brahmanas.

The ground that slopes toward the east, is red in color, adorned with *kuśa* and *daba* grass, and possesses the fragrance of blood, is praised for Kṣatriyas. The ground that possesses a slope toward the south, is adorned with *kuśa* and *daba* grass, and has the fragrance of food, is indeed praised for Vaiśyas. The ground that possesses a slope toward the west, is endowed with *dūrvā* grass, and has the fragrance of wine, is declared suitable for Śūdras. A mound elevated toward the east brings about the destruction of sons; one elevated toward the southeast (the fire-quarter) bestows wealth.

From this point onward, the entire reading in the manuscript differs as follows: "In the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*), if the northeast (*agni*) is low, there will be loss of wealth; if the south (*yāmya*) is high, it brings freedom from disease; if the southwest (*nirṛti*) is high, it brings gain of fortune; if the west (*varuṇa*) is high, it bestows sons. If the northwest (*vāyu*) is high, there is loss of property; if the north (*saumya*) is high, there is illness. One should know that the northeast (*īśāna*) brings great prosperity—this is the sequence for the *vāstu*. Furthermore, one learned in the scriptures should know the trees according to their colors: the *aśvattha* tree is auspicious in the east, and the *udumbara* in the south. (31–33)

The Nyagrodha tree is excellent in the west, and the Plakṣa is auspicious in the north. The Nyagrodha is desirable in the east, and the Plakṣa likewise in the south. The Aśvattha should be in the western part, and the Udumbara in the north. The Aśvattha causes fear of fire, while the Plakṣa causes negligence. The Nyagrodha brings about the stroke of a weapon, and the Udumbara causes disease of the belly. [One should avoid] wood, bricks, chaff, charcoal, stones, bones, and reptiles.

Having seen things excavated by Halāya, one should know this result therein: in the case of wood, there is fear of fire; in bricks, the arrival of wealth; (37) in charcoal, likewise disease; in husks, the loss of wealth; in stones, prosperity; and in bones, the destruction of the family. A dwelling site that slopes toward the north brings happiness to that family; as long as it is lower toward the east, it increases in wealth and grain; but for that which is lower toward the south, that family goes to ruin. (38)

A site sloping toward the east indeed prospers very quickly; it swiftly bestows happiness upon men and increases like the waxing moon. A site sloping toward the south brings certain physical ruin; for men, it diminishes rapidly like the moon in the dark fortnight. If it slopes toward the west, one suffers loss of wealth. A site sloping toward the north prospers like the waxing moon. One should likewise predict danger from reptiles for all such [sloped] sites.

Ground that is not saline, moist, praiseworthy, and abundant with water; that which is covered with grass and stones—such earth is esteemed in the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*). Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Characteristics of the Earth," in the Science of Architecture. Now begins the third chapter. Now I shall describe, in brief, the expansion of the sacrificial altar (*vedī*) for all [buildings], as well as the layout of the site (*vāstu*), the names [of the divisions], and the placement of the deities. A measurement of fifty *daṇḍas* or thirty is declared by the wise.

One should make the extent of the altar (vedī) for kings forty *daṇḍas* in width; it is proclaimed as being either thirty-two or thirty *daṇḍas*. Furthermore, the extent of the altar for the twice-born (*dvija*) is said to be thirty-three *daṇḍas*. The extent of the altar for Vaiśyas is stated by those skilled in the arts to be nineteen, twenty, or twenty-two *daṇḍas* in measurement. And the extent of the altar for Śūdras is declared to be twenty-five or twenty *daṇḍas*, or else fifteen *daṇḍas*.

5–6. The extent of the sacrificial ground (vedī) for kings and others has been described individually, according to their respective order, as superior, inferior, and middling. 7. Regarding the science of architecture (vāstuvidyā), I shall describe the determination of the directions when auspicious omens and so forth have occurred; specifically during the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa), in a month of the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), at a time of favorable rising [of planets]. Having made the site perfectly level on all sides, resembling a mirror, one should ensure it is level in the center, either by a staff-measure or by the presence of water.

Having placed a jar with a hole in its center, filled with a load of water, upon a support for the mechanism, one should set it down level in the middle of the ground. Then, when the ground has been evenly sprinkled with the water flowing out, one should know [the level] by the water according to whether its distribution is neither deficient nor excessive. Having made a small mark on the ground in the center, one should set a gnomon (śaṅku) upright there; it should be such that its base and top portions are equal, made from ivory or from hard wood, and fashioned in a circular shape.

A gnomon (*śaṅku*) that is equal, straight, free from defects, six-sided, level, and twelve *aṅgulas* in height is recommended here. Between the tail and the tip of the gnomon, one should fix two needles made of iron, equal in thickness and length, each as thick as a barley grain (*yava*). One should place a thread, as long as the gnomon, upon that point and, standing at that point, rotate it around to form a circle. Then, one should place that gnomon at the center of that circle during both [the morning and evening] suns.

Just as the tip of the gnomon's shadow touches the circumference of that circle in the forenoon at twenty-one [units] before its decrease, so too in the afternoon, when the shadow is emerging from the circle and touching that same line, one should mark it there as before. One should then stretch a thread between those two marks, measuring the distance from the center (arṣa) to the south (rakṣas). The Third Chapter. [This is done] by means of a gnomon made straight by a plumb-line placed within the circle of the earth established by the water-level method.

The two directions in which the sun enters and leaves its path belong to Varuṇa and Vāsava [the West and the East]. The sun moves along the southern and northern directions at every moment according to the circle of its apogee; therefore, that direction appears crooked, whereas it would be straight along the line of the obliquity of the ecliptic (apakramamaurvyām). The difference between the sines of the sun's amplitude at the times of the exit and entry of the shadow, multiplied by the hypotenuse (śravaṇa) and divided by the radius (lambaka), shall be the result in finger-breadths (aṅgula) and so forth.

Thereafter, one should move the point (bindu) from this [mark] by the solar transit in reverse order; or else, due to the precession of the equinoxes (āyana), one should shift the point eastward from the true east or west. Having placed a mark to the south of the eastern mark, that direction is called the direction of Indra (the east). Likewise, to the north of the eastern mark, that shall be the direction of Īśa (the north). Some say that in the construction of temples for Śiva and so forth, this is the east; others have declared that in the construction of dwellings for Brahmins and others, it is the direction of Indra. However, according to the observation of various Tantras, the direction of Brahmā alone is the east for everyone.

"In a place devoid of latitude, such as Laṅkā and the like, this determination regarding the sky [of the sun's position] would occur. Thus some have said; therefore, the distinction of places possessing latitude is now described, for there certainly exists a difference among places with latitude due to the sun’s shifting course. And it has been stated by others in the *Vāstuvidyā*: "Having fixed the eastern line on the ground as the straightest possible, and having formed a pair of compasses (matsya) in the southern direction using two lines drawn from the root and tip of that [eastern] line, one should then [fix] the thread..."

Having marked the directions and fixed the center here with threads, one should draw the lines from the corner-fish to form a square, as was previously prescribed for the layout of the site: "The width of the altar (vedi) and its length should be equal. Having thus made it a square, one should drop the threads there. (11) Having divided it into eighty-one squares, one who knows the division of the principles of Vāstu should establish the deities in their respective places, part by part. (12)

One should name the deity Brahmā, who resides in the center upon nine squares. Then, one should arrange four groups of six squares in the cardinal directions. Therein, those expert in the science of architecture (vāstu-vidyā) say there are eight groups of two squares each; these thirteen deities situated within have been declared. Furthermore, thirty-two [deities] situated outside have been mentioned by the architects. I shall also state the names of these deities: Parjanya, Jayanta, Mahendra, and Āditya.

Satya, Bhṛśa, and Antarikṣa; and there, Agni is likewise the eighth. [Note: This verse is seen as an additional line in some manuscripts. The third chapter: Pūṣan and Vitatha, as well as Gṛhakṣata and Yama; Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, Mṛga, and Nirṛti is the eighth. Dauvārika, Sugrīva, Puṣpadanta, and Vāruṇa; Asura, Śoṣaṇa, Roga, and Vāyu is likewise the eighth.

Nāga, Mukhya, Bhallāṭa, Soma, and Argala, as well as Aditi and Uditi, are situated in the northern direction. These, beginning with Parjanya, are to be known as the thirty-two deities stationed in a single step, arranged clockwise; these are the deities of the enclosure wall (prākāra). The deity named Aryaman is situated between Brahmā and Bhāskara; the one known as Vivasvān is remembered as being between Kṛtānta and Brahmā; and the deity named Mitra is between Varuṇa and Brahmā.

In the space between Brahmā and Soma, the deity known as Mahīdhara is remembered [to be placed]. Likewise, Āpa and Apavatsa, stationed upon two feet, should be established in due order between Brahmā and Śāna by the one performing the Vāstu rite. Between Hutāśa and Brahmā, the presiding deity named [Mahendra] is to be installed; Savitṛ and Sāvitra are likewise situated upon two feet each. Furthermore, in the Vāstu layout, Indra and Indrajaya are located between Nirṛti and Brahmā.

Those who know the science of architecture (vāstu-veda) declare that two [deities] are situated at each pair of feet. And it is proclaimed that the deities situated between Brahmā and Vāyu are [the others]. Rudra and Rudrajaya are proclaimed to be in the outer corners. The Third Chapter, titled "The Description of the Deities of Vāstu," in the Science of Architecture. Now begins the Fourth Chapter: Then one should construct two doors facing east, two facing south, two facing west, and two facing north.

In the Māhendra [quarter], a door facing east is praised among the learned classes; however, Jayanta has declared with certainty that the western door is likewise [recommended]. In Gṛhakṣata, a door is desired for Kṣatriyas; in Gandharva, a door is invariably desired by Vaiśyas as it bestows their welfare. In Puṣpadanta, the door is desired by Śūdras as it bestows their welfare; and in Sugrīva and Bhallāṭa, the door is suitable for all castes.

In the primary [direction], the door is fixed; that which is other than from Bhallāṭa is traditionally taught. Now I shall describe the fruit of the doors as proclaimed by the best among those who know Vāstu: (5) If the door is placed in Āditya, the destruction of sons then occurs. In Satya there is the breaking of friendships, and in Bhṛśa one is separated from her husband. (6) When the door is made in Antarikṣa, one goes even to ruin. If the door is placed in Pāvaka, the master of the house dies. (7)

If the door is constructed in the *pūṣan* (Pūṣan) position, one should perish through terrible wasting diseases; if the door is placed in the *vitatha* (Vitatha) position, one should predict the death of the master of the house. (8) If the door is made in the *gṛhakṣata* (Gṛhakṣata) position, there is an increase in prosperity; if the door is made in the *yama* (Yama) position, one should declare total ruin and death. (9) If the door is fashioned in the *gandharva* (Gandharva) position, there is an increase in all undertakings; if the door is in the *bhṛṅgarāja* (Bhṛṅgarāja) position, there is calamity; and if in the *mṛga* (Mṛga) position, there is the destruction of crops. (10) One should know that in the *nirṛti* (Nirṛti) position there is death, while in the *dauvārika* (Dauvārika) position there is speed [or success].

If Sugrīva is placed [at the gate], there shall be all gains; if Puṣpadanta, there will be virtue. (11) If Vāruṇa is established at the gate, there is fear from enemies or thieves. If Asura is established at the gate, it is a constant cause of deceit. (12) According to the science of architecture (vāstuvidyā), if Śoṣaṇa is established at the gate, one withers but does not perish. If Roga is made the gate, a man becomes afflicted with jaundice. (13) If a gate is made in the place of Vāta, a man is tormented by wind.

If the door is constructed at the *nāga* point, there will quickly be fear of serpents. If the door is made at the *mukhya* point, one immediately attains the status of a Brahmin. If the door is made at *bhallāṭa*, a man obtains the status of a Vaiśya. If the door is made at *soma*, he will become devoted to sacrifice. If the door is made at *argala*, a man dies by water. If the door is made at *aditi*, one should predict abdominal disease. And if the door is made at *uditi*, it brings about the destruction of the wife and the family.

17 || If the door is placed in the Rudra [direction], the house is consumed by fire; if in Parjanya, wealth shall perish; and if in Jayanta, one shall obtain victory. 18 || If the door is made in the Māhendra [direction], there is indeed greatness. The internal [spaces] have been described, and now the external door is being discussed. 19 || Where it is elevated, there the door should be; where it is low, there the house should be. One should not cause a door to be made in the eighth zodiac sign from the house. 20 ||

In the Māhendra, Gṛha, Phallāṭa, and Puṣpadantaka [sections], there should be great gates, as well as side-gates if they exist. In the Bhṛśa, Pūṣan, Bhṛṅga, Dauvāra, Śoṣa, Nāga, Diti, and Parjanya [sections], the water-channels should extend from Indra toward Īśa, ending at the bolt (argalā); these are auspicious when they slope toward the northeast. In the Sūrya [section] is the Sun; in Bhṛśa, Viṣṇu; in Agni, Kālī; in Yama, Guha; and in the middle of Viṣṇu and Varuṇa is the abode of Sugrīva and Sugata.

In the northeast (Īśāna) is the temple of the Jina; in the east, that of Vāyu; in the southeast (Agni), that of Caṇḍī; in the north, that of Kubera; and in the northwest (Vāyu), that of Mahākālī. In the west, that of the Mothers; in the southwest (Nirṛti), that of Aditi; and in the northeast (Īśāna), the temple of Cāmuṇḍī is recommended. Alternatively, the house of Vighneśa (Gaṇeśa) should be located in the southwest or in Jayanta (the northeast). Or, others have declared the arrangement of the deities as follows: the abode of Brahmā should be in the center of that village, city, or kingdom; or it may be in the east or west, facing Viṣṇu, Gaurī, and the others.

A temple of Śiva that faces away from the northeast (Aiśāna) is inauspicious for humans, whether it be self-manifested (*svayambhū*), divine, or of the sages (*ārṣa*), regardless of where it is situated. Even in such a case, it does not constitute a fault; however, those seeking auspiciousness should avoid facing it with their backs. The abode of Gaurī should be in the east, in the northeast, or in the center; likewise for Sūrya and Śrī. The temple of the Mothers should be in the south, that of the Teacher (Śāstṛ) and Kālī in the southwest (*nairṛta*). The temple of Ṣaṇmukha should be in the west (*vāruṇa*), and immediately thereafter, that of Jyeṣṭhā.

In the north-west, the north, or within the domain of the World-Guardians (Lokapālas), or between Indra, Īśāna, and Soma, one should establish the abode of the Kṣetrapāla. In this manner, it brings prosperity to countries, villages, cities, and the like. To the south or east of the cow-pen, or likewise to the north of the Vaiśya quarter, water is auspicious everywhere; to the north, a flower garden; to the south, a grove for courtesans; and all around, dwellings for those of Śūdra birth. To the east of the Vaiśyas and merchants, there should be the royal highway in the center.

To the northeast, there should be the houses of potters and boatmen; in the north, those of basket-makers; in the northwest, the house of slaughterers; in the west, that of oil-sellers; and in the north, that of carpenters—or else in the northwest or southeast. In the northwest, there should be the dwellings of artisans and the like; in the west, those of weavers. Two *krośas* or one *krośa* outside [the city], the settlement of the *caṇḍālas* should be located. To the northeast, beyond one *krośa*, should be the cremation ground (*pitṛvana*). For others not mentioned here, one should arrange their residence according to reason.

In the capital city, the king’s residence is located in the Aparāṃśaka division, which is a portion of Brahmā. To its east is the outer enclosure, provided with the Indrakośa assembly hall. The kitchen is in the Antarikṣa [Agni] sector; the bedchamber is in the Gṛharakṣaka [Yama] sector; and the armory is in the Nirṛti sector. The dining hall is in the Varuṇa sector; the recreation hall is in the Vāyu sector; and the treasury is in the Phalāṭa [Kubera] sector. Likewise, the cowshed is in the Saumya [Soma] sector, or it is recorded as being in the Argala [Nairṛta] sector. The bathhouse is in the Parjanya sector, and the house for fire-offerings and worship is in the Aiśāna [Īśāna] sector.

The dance hall should be for the Gandharvas, while the elephant stable is for Pūṣan. For the Dityas, Adityas, and Turāṇas, as well as for women, it should be in the north-west. In the center, one should construct a water-stall pavilion (prapā-maṇḍapa) or any other suitable structure according to the circumstances. For Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and even wealthy men, the temple types to be described hereafter are the abodes of prosperity. However, for those who are unable [to build the full type], those [simplified versions] constructed with appropriate adaptations are recommended. Thus it is stated in the Īśānagurudevapaddhati.

A pond should be constructed in the Māhendra quarter, and a well in the Īśāna; a kitchen in the Parjanya or Agni quarter, and a dining hall in front of that; a water-cistern in the Nairṛta quarter, a granary in the Varuṇa quarter, and a cow-pen in the Śiva or Vāyu quarter; and a house for the mortar and pestle in the Vāyu quarter. Now, he describes the specific arrangement for their royal residence: the Brahmā-house is in the center, the king’s residence in the Mitra quarter, a pleasure garden in the Anila quarter, a gymnasium in the Ula quarter, wealth in the Dhanapati quarter, and bathing facilities in the Parjanya quarter.

The Fourth Chapter Just as [the house] presides over the abode of enjoyment in the northeast (Īśa), dance and so forth in Varuṇa, the science of music and so forth in Nirṛti, and the bedchamber for kings in the position of Gṛhakṣata; then, having passed from the center of the courtyard by a distance measured by four, five, six, seven, and so on [units], one should place the gate suitable for public traffic in the position of Puṣpadantika. Furthermore, large gates and side doors should be placed in Phalgu, Gṛhakṣata, and others, such as Aṣṭa, Śānta, Bhṛśa, and the rest, extending all around up to Parjanya.

Thus it is stated in the *Pañcāśikā*: "From the thread extending south to north, one should [measure] eight fingers' breadth to the west, within the space between Brahma and Vayu. There, the location for the pillar situated in the house of Scorpio (Khalari) is determined. Then, having divided the section of Ishana into four parts as well, the wise man should fashion the zodiacal wheel (*rāśicakra*) in the section of Ishana. Therein, the digging of wells is most excellent in Capricorn and Cancer; some scholars, however, perform it in Scorpio and Taurus."

One should construct the animal-shed in the *vāstu* between the bull and the *kartī*. On the ground to the west, at a distance of one *daṇḍa* from the *yama-sūtra*, and in the intermediate space between Yama and Vāyu, one should construct the dwelling for the mortar (*ulūkhala*). One should avoid the line extending east-west from the pillar situated at the western end of the bow-shaped [enclosure]; following that line, one should construct [the shed] on both sides. One should also avoid the location of a well, and likewise another such spot from that [well]. A door is desired in the zodiac signs of Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn.

Whether the site-sutra extends from east to west or from south to north, one should divide the building site (*vāstu*) into nine parts; five parts are on the south side, while three parts are set aside on the left (north) side, and the door is prescribed for the remainder. Thus it is stated in another text. Regarding the inquiry into wells: "If the position [of the well] falls under Cancer, Virgo, Libra, Sagittarius, Scorpio, Capricorn, or Pisces, it is said to be auspicious water. In the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*): "A well situated in Aquarius is excellent, while those in Pisces and Aries are middling."

The wise know that when the *adhana* (the sign of Capricorn) is situated in a well, it is indeed like a well itself. Furthermore, there are two inferior types of wells based on external movement; these are called the "two wells. Moreover, another pair of wells is said to be outside the enclosure wall. That which they call the "well situated in Aries" (*meṣastha*) is known as water that is heavy and smiling in measurement. When Aquarius or Pisces is in the well, the water is light and beautiful; it removes mental suffering and increases sons and grandsons. Likewise, when the well is situated externally, it is free from both virtues and defects.

One should know that poison resides in the uneven lines and nectar is said to reside in the nectar-line. One should know the destruction of the lineage when [the thread] stands upon the lineage-line, and the mixing of castes when it stands upon the pillar-line. Death occurs when it is on the karma-thread, and loss of memory when it is on the threads outside the karma-thread. The wise know that thieves, enemies, and domestic calamities reside in the house-thread; they are outside the enclosure-wall thread, in the domain of the Śūdras. Furthermore, there are four houses in the four corners; they say these are square, and I shall now tell you their application.

One should arrange for food, snacks, and drinks in the *mīnagocara* (fish-range) area; likewise, the stationing of cows should be in the *yugma* (pair), while that of buffaloes is in the *dānava* (demon) area. There, grains are brought in, or one may have a pavilion (*prasāda*) constructed. In the *vāyavya* (north-west) direction, the placement of the mortar and pestle for rice is also located. If the builder wishes to contract the space due to a specific need, they know that the layout of each individual house consists of two squares. In the center of the square-shaped structure, the pavilion is said to be situated.

If the master should contract [the house] out of a desire for some purpose, then there will be fear, food, and drink in the eastern part of the house; in the southern part, wealth, grain, and so forth, as well as a bed, are ordained. Furthermore, it is traditionally taught that the stationing of cows should be made there. Chapter Four. [The placement of deities] is proclaimed for Brāhmaṇas in Gṛhakṣata, Māhendra, Mahīdhara, Soma, as well as Phallāṭa and Argala. 21.

The bedchamber should be constructed with its auspicious ridge facing the east; one should construct the great kitchen in the intermediate space (Antarikṣa) and in Navadvāra. One should especially always construct the fodder storehouse in Vitatha, the cow-pen in Asura, and the salt storehouse in Gandharva. At the gate of the Vaiśya, Phalgu and Puṣpadanta are praised; Yama is declared for Vivasvat, and Gṛhakṣata for Gandharva.

The learned should construct the bed with its head toward the east; the path should be in the east or the west (Vāruṇa), or the kitchen may be as previously described. The Gandharva quarter should be the site for the dwelling, and likewise the Asura quarter for the cow-pen. The Pitṛ quarter should be the site for the womb-chamber (garbha-bhūmi); thus it has been declared by those who know the science of architecture (vāstu-vid). In the west should be the wealth, grain, and so forth, as well as the bed and the recreation area; or else, Śaṅkara says that the grains are brought there.

In the northern part of the site for the house, recreation is prescribed; there, Vācaspati likewise mentions the pestle and mortar. Alternatively, Brahmā has declared that the courtyard should be in the center. This is the opinion of all the gods. Water contained in a jar is best; that in a fish-sign (Mīna) is middling; and in Capricorn (Makara) or Taurus (Vṛṣa), it is inferior for a village or a dwelling. Thus it is stated in the Īśānagurupaddhati. In the science of architecture (Vāstuvidyā), the gates of Śūdra are worshipped at Phallāṭa and Mahendra.

Sugrīva, Puṣpadanta, Mitra, and Varuṇa likewise; it is the established rule that the bedchamber should be located there for all [the deities]. The measurement for the gatekeeper's chamber is said to be the paternal ground-measure. The kitchen should be in the region of Pūṣan, and the cow-pen in the region of Asura. One should especially always establish the place for perfumes in the region of Gandharva. Whatever has been stated regarding the width and length of the altar (vedī), that same measurement should apply here as well.

Having thus made it square, one should draw a thread through its center. With two threads—one directed eastward and the other curved northward—the altar (vedi) shall be formed with four divisions, known respectively as Brāhma and Yāmya. Furthermore, the wise know the names of the regions starting from the northeast to be Mānuṣya, Yāmya, Daiva, and Āsura. Indeed, some maintain that the place for humans is in the Mānuṣya region, while the place for the lords is in the Daiva region.

The two [squares] in the south-east and the north-west are censurable for men in the rite of house-building. (33) Having resolved upon that ground, one should then construct a large altar (*vedikā*) and perform the worship of Vāstu. Having further divided the ground into sixty-four squares, one should then lay down two threads at the corners. (34) Chapter Four. Therein reside fifty-three deities within the body of Vāstu; one should worship them in due order. Their distribution is now being declared. (31)

Brahmā is established in the central four-square [cell]; in the cardinal directions stand those with two squares; outside of that, four [deities] are situated in the intermediate corners, each occupying one square; furthermore, sixteen deities occupy half-squares in the corners; likewise, sixteen deities occupy two squares in the outer cardinal directions, and eight occupy two squares in the outer intermediate directions. [These are: Īśāna, Parjanya, Jayanta, Śakra, Dhvānta, Apaḥ, Satya, Bhṛśa, Antarikṣa, Agni, Pūṣan, Vitatha, Ambu, Gṛhakṣata, Pretanivāsa, and Bhaṭṭāraka (Yama). || 36–37 ||

Then Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, and he who is named Mṛga are the praised Pitṛs; Dauvārika is situated between the west and the east, followed by Sugrīva and Puṣpadanta. Again, Varuṇa is highly praised, along with Asura, Śoṣa, Roga, Pavana, and Bhujaṅga; then Mukhya, Bhallāṭa, and Niśākara, followed again by Argala and Āditya in this sequence. These thirty-two, having entered the outer positions of the supporting pillars (viṣkambha), are thus prescribed all around.

I shall describe the eight [deities] to be placed in the half-padas of the intermediate corners, and the four to be joined in the cardinal directions. In the science of Vāstu: Savitṛ is in the south-east; Brahmā is between Agni and the fire [corner]; Indra and Indrajaya are well known as situated in the half-padas in the south-west; Rudra and Rudrajaya pervade the north-west; likewise, Āpa and Apavatsa are situated as a pair in the north-east. || 40-41 ||

In the directions starting from the east, there shall be Dvipāda, Āryaka, and likewise Vivasvān; then Mitra and Mahīdhara in the west, while Brahmā stands in the center upon four squares. (42) I shall now describe those situated outside in the cardinal and intermediate directions in order: Śarva, Skanda, Aryamā, Īśa, Jambhaka, and Pilipiñchaka. (43) Having established Carakī, Vidārī, Pūtanā, and Pāparākṣasī, one should worship these [deities] within the sixty-four squares. (44)

Thus, the syllables divided into groups of eight occupy the positions; Brahmā is situated in the center within four squares, while the four [deities] placed in the directions are outside him, each occupying four squares. Two [squares] are located in the corners, likewise two occupy a single square, and two by two are situated in half-squares. Outside in the directions, there are two by two occupying two squares, while the remaining [deities] are established in a single square each. Alternatively, when arranged in eighty-one squares, one should worship the deities; therein, Pitāmaha (Brahmā) remains occupying nine squares in the center. [End of] Chapter Four.

Then, having resorted to the path of these [deities] and having envisioned a single site for them, the wise one should likewise properly conceive of those deities within its constituent parts and worship them thoroughly. (16) Formerly, there was a cruel asura who caused fear to all the worlds and was exceedingly arrogant due to the strength of his arms; now, struck down upon the surface of the earth and conquered by the gods, he has become peaceful and exists as the Vāstupuruṣa situated in a square. (47)

Then, his head was placed upon Īśa; his two feet were stationed in the directions of Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Hutāśana (Agni); his two elbows were fixed upon his arms; and the palms of his hands were cast upon his chest, thereby making him lie face upwards upon the limbs of the deities, as I shall describe. In the two outer enclosures, two two-legged deities are situated at each corner; in their center and around them, six six-legged deities are located, and four are positioned in the cardinal directions in due order.

One should arrange thirty-two deities in single-file rows within the outer enclosure, starting with Īśa and others, positioned in the directions beginning from the East. Then, in the corners starting from the Southeast (Agni), one should place eight deities in sequence beginning with Sāvitra; likewise, the remaining ones are situated around the perimeter in the cardinal directions.

The meaning is "the Vāstupuruṣa. In the science of architecture (Vāstuvidyā), his lord is situated on the head; likewise, Parjanya and Udit are in the right and left eyes, and the Waters (Āpaḥ) are established again in the mouth. Furthermore, Āpavatsa should be placed in his neck; then, Jayanta and Aditi are to be placed on his two shoulders. Again, Mahendra and the others, beginning with Argala, are to be established in order upon his two arms.

Sāvitra, Rudra, Savitṛ, and Jaya should likewise be situated upon the two forearms (50). Brahmā is placed at the navel, and the noble Mahīdhara is established upon the two breasts; Vivasvat and Mitra are likewise in the belly, and the Pitṛs are seated upon the two feet (51). Indra is in the penis, and Indrajaya is subsequently seated upon the two testicles; one should worship these correctly with their respective names preceded by the *praṇava* (Om) and accompanied by mantra (52).

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Configuration of the Vāstupuruṣa," in the Science of Architecture (Vāstuvidyā). One should construct a grid of sixty-four squares using human-sized units. In the center, there is a four-square area for the auspicious pavilion of Brahmā. One enclosure is prescribed with twelve squares; another enclosure, moreover, is provided with eight squares. Therein one should construct a dwelling with a width measured by those squares; its length should be made twice that [width], and this is known as the human enclosure.

That *paiśācī* [arrangement] consisting of twenty-eight squares would be censurable; it should be the third enclosure (*āvṛti*), and one should not construct a house there. Now, in the divine (*daivikī*) enclosure, one should cause a temple to be built for men. A layout equal in measure to the square is called "two-padas" (*dvipada*). The height of the base should be equal to the width of the house; thus, being three-quarters or one-and-a-half [of that], it shall be excellent, inferior, or middling. Alternatively, one may arrange the site as a perfect square of sixteen squares (*pada*).

In that regard, the temple is situated in the south-western corner (Nairṛti) within the divine section (daivika-khaṇḍa). One should construct the most excellent site extending from Nairṛti to Īśa (the north-east) in the human section (mānuṣya-khaṇḍa); even in the human section, the position of Nairṛti is indeed suitable for the dwelling. That is declared to be the human [section] where there is a group of four squares in the northeast; the divine section is said to consist of a group of four squares in the south-western corner. It is proclaimed as the demonic (āsura) [section] when it is in the northwest; thus, this house in the southeast corner is without divisions.

The two sections, the Asura and the Yāmya, are censurable; the Daiva and Mānuṣa sections are to be joined together. (10) In that regard, there may be sixty-four, eighty-one, or one hundred squares. A wise man should construct his temple according to whichever among these he prefers. (11) One should make the thickness of the enclosure wall (*vṛti*) on the outside equal to its width; the thickness of the *sautra* [enclosure] should be half of that, and the thickness of the *talima* [platform] should be made equal to that [thickness of the *sautra*]. (12)

And there, one should construct a grove that resembles a gatehouse; or one should construct a stone embankment (*palidha*) as level as a baked brick. Or one may make a fence with thorny branches, or make it impassable for a camel’s eye. Among these, the grove is considered superior, and the embankment is likewise declared to be middling. The inferior [type] is a covering of branches; of these, one should choose whichever is easily available. A wise man should plant trees in all directions within the enclosure.

The *panasa* (jackfruit) is excellent in the east, the *kramuka* (areca nut) in the south, and the *kera* (coconut) in the west. In the north, the mango (*cūta*) is auspicious; furthermore, the *nāga* and *kesara* (flowering trees) are likewise excellent in the east.
The Tintriṇī has been declared for the east, and the umbrella-bearing tree (chatrī) is said to be the best in the west; if there are trees with inner pith within, let them likewise be so situated.

Those trees which have bark as their essence should also be situated entirely on the exterior; those trees whose entire substance is solid wood should be planted in all directions. It is not desired that trees devoid of pith should exist within the precincts [of the temple]. Creepers such as the *jāti* and *nāga*, as well as plantain trees (*rambhā*), are auspicious everywhere. Since it has been stated that even the *hāṭaka* tree is not desired in the vicinity of the temple, therefore all trees at the extremities of every direction should be beyond reproach.

The temple should be situated in the direction presided over by the lord of the quarter where the door is placed; it may have one story or two stories, and in the case of two stories, it may have two faces or no face at all. The placement of the door-pillars is declared by the best of artisans to be according to the [subject’s] birth [sign]; the path leading from the entrance to the base should be sloping, corresponding to the width of that door. When the width is multiplied by four (the number of oceans), the resulting [figure] shall be the [temple's] own *yoni* (source). This pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) should measure four *kiṣkus*, or it may be measured in *mātras*.

One should construct the enclosure (tati) at the gate presided over by one's own direction, or likewise along the path; the teachers say that the path should also be made thus at the courtyard gate. Thus ends the fifth chapter, named "The Arrangement of the Altar," in the Science of Architecture (Vāstuvidyā). Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the courtyard (aṅgaṇa). The courtyard has its origin in the Banner (dhvaja); it is joined with the length of the front entrance. The wise know that the courtyard is the area outside the footstools (pādukās).

"The banner is successful everywhere"—such is the illustration from the scriptures. (2) The numbers nine, two, twelve, eight, six, five, three, and four [should be used] for the house, the courtyard, the work, and the ocean [respectively]; likewise, the length of the courtyard should be made according to what is appropriate. (3) One should avoid piercing the centers of the houses, as it causes the destruction of the lineage. In the case of houses situated in the major directions, one should proceed clockwise by way of one's own path. (4) This must certainly be avoided by those possessed of skillful intelligence. There should be no intersection of the corner-lines in the middle of the corner-houses. (5)

This [measurement] becomes inauspicious; it should be avoided according to its own length. Rudras (11), randhras (9), adris (7), and bāṇas (5) are recorded as the steps for the fingers in sequence. (6) In a sixty-four-square grid, the thread for the house-work portion should be one-eighth; in an eighty-one-square grid, it is one-sixteenth; and in a hundred-square grid, it is one-twentieth. (7) One must avoid piercing the threads through the middle of the pillars and other such parts. Vital points (*marmas*) and other prohibited areas are manifoldly described in the work on architecture (*vāstu*). (8)

The Sixth Chapter. I shall now briefly describe those [faults] which are of two kinds; these also must be diligently avoided in pillars, walls, and so forth. (9) There are ten channels (nāḍīs) situated in the Vāstu, extending from the east toward the north within the eighty-one squares that have been laid out; one should draw lines with them along the diagonals. Here, the cords (rajju) situated around the three-and-a-half-square areas on their sides—I shall explain the various vital points (marmas) and so on by dividing them through those channel-cords. (10)

Dharma, Yaśovatī, Bhadrā, Śubhadā, Kāmadā, Śubhā, Citrā, Saumyā, Sudhā, and Gaurī—these ten channels (nāḍīs) face the east. Amṛtā, Vāruṇī, Śāntā, Hlādinī, Brahmavādinī, Manoramā, Rati, Kāntā, and Jvālinī—these face the north. Where there is a junction of eight [channels] mixed with the cords of the channels, there is a great vital point (mahāmarman) at the corner of the Brahma-sthāna. In each direction there are hexagons, and triangles exist on the sides.

Due to the conjunction of the two channels (nāḍī), those secondary vital points (upamarman) exist; there are twenty-four sets of four channel-vital points (nāḍīmarmāṇi). From the two cords (rajjū), there are four sets of nine cord-vital points (rajjumarmāṇi). One should point out the three located at the corners up to the end of the secondary vital points on the exterior. There is a junction of six vital points, and the total for the six is sixty. In the science of architecture (vāstuvidyā), there are five, and two joints of vital points (marmasandhi) in each of the four directions.

The vital point (marman) situated in the middle of the *pada* is free from defects when [aligned] with the two cords. In the procedure for constructing a house, a wise man must never damage these locations of the *vāstu*; for if they are damaged, there will be suffering for the king, the subjects, the Brahmins, and the cattle. Furthermore, it brings harm to the builder, the artisans, one's own children, wife, brothers, and relatives. Therefore, I shall now describe separately and in detail the specific defects resulting from piercing these locations. If the head, the mouth, the throat, or the heart are pierced, death shall occur.

If [the mark] is pierced on the chest, there will be heart disease; on the feet, there will be quarrels. On the forehead, there will be the loss of brothers; on the backs of the fingers, the destruction of wealth. On the thighs, there will be death for kinsmen, or perhaps the loss of one's wife. If it is located in the private parts, there will be the loss of sons; in the *aṣṭaka* (eight-pointed) area, there is the miscarriage of the fetus. In the *ṣaṭka* (six-pointed) area, there is increase; in the *catuṣka* (four-pointed), the destruction of relatives. In the *pañcaka* (five-pointed), disease is indicated; in the *trika* (three-pointed), there is danger from thieves.

One should avoid the junction of pipes, ropes, and so forth within the middle of a wall (22). Whatever has been mentioned or left unsaid, if it should occur through negligence, one should bury these items during the construction work (*vāstukarma*) for the sake of pacifying faults (23). [The word] "in the four" (*catasṛṣu*) should be supplied. This is the sixth chapter. The heads of a lion, an elephant, a buffalo, a tortoise, and a boar, fashioned from pure gold, shall bring prosperity to the house of the builder (24).

I shall describe [the layout] by means of sixty-four squares; one should draw lines for the veins at the corners of the site. One should draw three bamboo-lines (vaṃśas) reaching toward the east and the north, and three reaching toward the center and the corners. Those entering the squares of Mahendra and Dharmeśa, those entering the squares known as Gṛhakṣata and Āpya, those situated in the squares of Puṣpa, Danta, and Indu, and those situated in Phallāṭa and Mitra—these are the secondary bamboo-lines (anuvaṃśas). Three lines situated on the exterior in the four directions are known as the junctions (sandhis).

The vital points (*marmāṇi*), the junctions of the sutures, and the secondary vital points (*upamarma*) are situated at the feet. (27) The head, the mouth, the navel, the chest, and the heart are called the great vital points (*mahāmarmāṇi*). The junction of the two spinal columns is called the *lāṅgala*. (28) Piercing the head results in the loss of cattle; piercing the spine brings about death. Piercing the junction leads to exile, while piercing the spinal column brings danger. (29) Piercing the *triśūla* results in the loss of offspring; piercing the *haṅgala* causes headache. Piercing the *catuṣka* results in the destruction of vehicles; piercing the *ṣaṭka*, however, leads to many enemies.

30 || If [the house] is pierced at a *mahāmarma* (major vital point), the death of the master occurs; if pierced at an *upamarman* (minor vital point), there will be the destruction of brothers and sons. 31 || Furthermore, if pierced at a *marman* (vital point) according to the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*), the destruction of the builder's household is certain. One should avoid all defects prohibited in other treatises. 32 || Thus ends the sixth chapter in the science of architecture, titled "The Arrangement of the Vital Points of the House. Now begins the seventh chapter.

One should place a lion in Libra and Scorpio, a deer in Sagittarius and Aquarius, and an elephant in Aries and Taurus; in Leo, one should establish the abode of the banner (the serpent). In Virgo, the serpent lies with its head toward the east and its tail toward the south. In Sagittarius, it has its head toward the south and its tail toward the west. In Pisces, it has its head toward the west. Then, in Gemini, it likewise has its head toward the north and its tail toward the north. Thus, it rolls about in this manner through the ten months in succession.

Indeed, pillars should not be erected within the various parts of a human dwelling; if they do so, those staying there will certainly go to hell. (4) Diggṛhas (corner-houses) must never be constructed when the Sun is situated in either of the two signs [of Gemini or Libra]; if one does so, he goes to hell along with his servants, sons, and wealth. (5) When the Sun has ascended a sign, that person who is the form of the Vāstu deity wanders about, having placed his feet upon that [sign], his head resting on it, or lying on his left side. (6)

If there is loss of wealth at the foot, death at the head, misfortune at the back, and destruction at the chest or thighs, one should place the primary pillar in the belly for auspicious results. A three-winged house (triśālaka) lacking the northern wing is called *hiraṇyanābha*; it bestows wealth. A house lacking the eastern wing is named *sukṣetra*; it grants prosperity. A three-winged house lacking the southern wing is called *śūla*; it causes the destruction of wealth.

This [house], devoid of the eastern and western wings, brings about the death of sons and enmity. (8) A house that lacks both the eastern and western wings is called a *gṛhacullī*. The Lord of Speech (*Vāgadhipa*) says that a house lacking the southern and northern wings is a *siddhārthaka*. (9) A wing on the west and south is called *yamapa*; a wing on the west and north is termed *daṇḍa* by the ancients who know the treatises on architecture (*śilpaśāstra*). (10) A wing on the north and east is called *vāta*, and a wing on the east and south is [also so called].

This has been declared by the ancients who were experts in the science of architecture (śilpa-śāstra) as the deity Yamadevatā. In the *Siddhārtha* [section], there is the attainment of wealth; in the *Yamaśūrpa*, death for the householder; in that called *Daṇḍa*, death by the rod (execution); and in the *Gṛhacumhri*, quarrel and agitation. In the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*), in the section called *Vāta*, there is danger from wind; in that named *Yamadevatā*, there is death. Having understood all this and other such matters, those houses should be established accordingly. If there is one southern wing, or two, in the south and west...

The three-winged [temple] is joined with the northern wing, and the four-winged is provided with a banner. (14) The best temple has a length of eighteen cubits plus nine finger-breadths (aṅgulas), and a width of six cubits plus three finger-breadths. (15) It should be thirteen cubits long and nine finger-breadths wide; its breadth is four cubits plus eleven finger-breadths. (16) A temple of the lion-type is proclaimed as the middling one. For the smallest [type], one should make the length nine cubits plus nine finger-breadths. (17)

A house measuring three cubits and two fingers in width, facing the southern direction, with its entrance on the side of Puṣpadanta, likewise bestows prosperity upon Vaiśyas. (18) For those of the lowest caste (Haratas), the length is fifteen fingers; a dwelling of five cubits and five fingers in the west is excellent. (19) The length for a middle-class house is fifteen fingers and ten cubits, while its width is thirteen fingers and three cubits, having the bull as its source. (20) The length for the smallest house is stated to be fifteen fingers and six cubits.

A door measuring twelve *aṅgulas* [in height] and three cubits (*hasta*) in width, possessing five types of openings, is proclaimed for Śūdras. A house [for them] should be ten cubits in length and provided with finger-breadths (*aṅguli*). An elephant stable of the superior type is five cubits in width and seven *aṅgulas* [in height], likewise ten cubits in length and provided with finger-breadths. A width of fifteen *aṅgulas* and three cubits is declared to be the medium [size].

The house should have its fingers joined by the *samid* [measure] and be five cubits in length. For Brāhmaṇas, the door is prescribed to be at the *māhendra* position, with a width of one cubit less one finger (*kaniṣṭha*). The length of that eastern chamber is three fingers and fifteen cubits; its width is proclaimed for the best [type of house] as one finger and five cubits. However, the length of the middle [type of house] should be three fingers and nine cubits.

The width of the flagstaff (*dhvaja-mandira*) is said to be three times its thickness; [for the medium type] it is six cubits long and three finger-breadths wide. The wise know that for the smallest flagstaff, the width should be one finger-breadth and two cubits long. When a house is constructed primarily according to the *vala* (strength) direction, the door should be placed in the *Gṛhakṣata* direction; this is prescribed for a Kṣatriya. Thus ends the seventh chapter on the rules of time in the Science of Architecture (*Vāstu-vidyā*).

The houses of men are said to be the Vasus situated in the cardinal directions; they should be known as fivefold according to their arrangement and dimensions. (1) Situated in the cardinal and intermediate directions with extensions from their own source, that which has distinct wings (*bhinnaśālā*) is declared to bestow auspiciousness upon men. (2) That which is established in a single source in the cardinal and intermediate directions, and likewise by its perimeter, is to be known as the *caturaśālā* (four-winged house) by those who perceive the teachings of the architectural treatises (*śilpaśāstra*). (3) And that which is joined to a desired direction as its source, being uniform in its perimeter, [is also so classified].

A quadrangular [temple] should be known as having four equal sides, or it may be a single-winged structure that is elongated. (4) Because of the possibility of contact upon the entrance of Śūdras, women who have recently given birth, and others, one should avoid these two types within the abode of a Brāhmaṇa, even if they fall under the same shadow. (5) A quadrangular temple is distinguished by its name according to the presence of the Banner (dhvaja) in the corners, the measurement of the directions in the cardinal points, and so forth; however, that which is divided [irregularly] is not desired for the house of a Brāhmaṇa. (6) In the cardinal directions, the shapes should be joined with their own origins (yoni), and likewise connected to their own widths; in the corners, they should be joined with those origins, while at the perimeter, the Banner-origins should be present. (7)

That which is known by the name Bhinnaturyaśraka is approved even for a Brāhmaṇa; indeed, a house with separate halls (bhinnaśālā) bestows auspiciousness upon all social classes (varṇas). (8) I shall describe its characteristics briefly for the benefit of those of dull intellect. The intermediate spaces (antarāla), numbering eight (the Vasus), create divisions between the cardinal and intermediate directions. (9) The wise know that their excessive width leads to the destruction of wealth; they understand this well. When these [spaces] are too narrow, there is disease; therefore, one should avoid them. (10) The width of the intermediate space should be determined according to the breadth of the house.

Likewise, when there is an excess of the interval, they know that [the pillar] to be thick within that space. (11) That which is less than the thickness of its own axis is called "contraction. Joints of pillars should not be made in the middle of their own diameter or length. (12) A joint situated on the diagonal axis leads to death. Now, I shall explain the determination of rows of pillars based on their intersection. (13) In that regard, odd numbers are known as rows, while even numbers are prescribed for the pillars and so forth.

Those whose delight is directed toward the lower parts are proclaimed as "milk" (payas). An excess of that [height] leads to destruction for the temple of the tree, the lotus, and the cow. Now, one should cause the width of the base (pāda) to be made according to its length; it is constructed with proportions derived from the mountains (seven), the earth (one), the doors (four), the rows (ten), and the Rudras (eleven). One should make the extension of the upper parts equal to that, and likewise for the subsequent ones. Its thickness, however, is half of that, and is known by the name Rūpottara. When the thickness is made with five parts, its molding (vājana) is twice that.

One should make the *ghana* (the solid block) three parts, and the *paṭṭaniṣka* (the fillet and protrusion) likewise; this may be equal [to the *ghana*], or one-quarter less, or half, in all types of buildings (*vāstu*). The reduction at the top of the pillar (*stambhāgra*) should be one-eighth part or more. From the base, the bottom portion (*mūlāgra*) should be three times the length of the base-shaft (*mūladaṇḍa*), or even one-and-a-half times. According to the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*), one may also make it four times; this is called the "middle octagonal" form. The upper tip of the shaft is one unit, while the pinnacle (*śikhā*) is known to be one-third of that.

Now I shall describe the [auspicious] dimensions of houses and other structures; I shall not [describe] their long and wide measurements. The banner (dhvaja), lion (siṃha), bull (vṛṣa), and elephant (hastin)—these indeed are the deities of the cardinal directions. Smoke (dhūma), dog (śvan), donkey (khara), and crow (dhvāṅkṣa) are known as the lords of the intermediate directions. Among these, the banner and the others are considered auspicious, while smoke and the others are remembered as inauspicious. One unit is said to be the banner, two are called smoke, three are the lion, four are the dog, and five are declared to be the bull.

The six, the seven, the eight, and the nine are declared to be the *khara*, *mātaṅga*, *dhvāṅkṣa*, and so forth; these are remembered as the birth-classes (*yoni*) of houses and other structures, starting from the eastern direction in sequence. (24) When the desired length is doubled and increased by one part of that [length], and then increased by one part of the multiplier of the desired *yoni*, it is called the *paryanta*. (25) Having multiplied that by eight, and then divided by twelve, fifteen, eighteen, and twenty-seven, the remainders are remembered as the sequence [of the *yoni*]. (26)

The lunar days (tithis), asterisms (tārās), weekdays (vāras), and their respective nāḍīs are also taken into account; therein, the result derived from the asterism is declared by the teachers to be the [person's] age. From childhood until death, this is determined by that very result. Having multiplied it by three and divided by thirty-eight (the number of Indra and the Vasus), the remainder becomes the expenditure (vyaya) and the source (yoni) respectively. May there be no Viṣṭi or a yoga of death among the abodes of men; for one situated in an abode of a death-yoga quickly goes to the abode of Yama.

The *viṣṭi* [muhūrta] leads to total destruction; therefore, one should avoid those two. The conjunctions of childhood and old age, as well as the *riktā* [tithis], are also censured; nevertheless, they may be accepted by those who discern what is appropriate and inappropriate. That which remains when half of the diameter is subtracted is called the "width" (*vistāra*). Alternatively, having multiplied the circumference by those [proportional] parts, the length and width are established; this is known as the "triple-width" (*guṇavyāsa*). The numbers beginning with eight (*vasu*) and ending with the vision (*darśana*) are thus proclaimed.

33–36. Vyāsa states that each of those four [dimensions] must be made in accordance with the requirements of the housework. Among the six [measures] beginning with Vasu (eight) and increasing by four, a reduction of one-quarter is prescribed. Those [measures] declared to be deficient by one-quarter should be avoided in human dwellings. A reduction of one-quarter leads to the destruction of the lineage; a deficiency in length leads to death; an excess in length leads to ruin; while the desired length brings wealth. Therefore, one should not allow any increase or decrease from the specified cubits. There is no fault in using finger-breadths (aṅgula), except in both cases when it concerns full cubits.

The various types of *yoni* (wombs) for Tārā and the other deities are to be fashioned by them, as previously described. I shall now briefly explain the junctions, the ritual actions, and the designations: a short substance is placed on the left, while a long substance is on the right. In the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*), these should be applied in sequence at the side of the *kīla* (stake) on the right. The length of the joint-section is said to be equal to its own width; alternatively, one may make it half that or less than a quarter, according to what is appropriate or inappropriate.

And at the joint of the tree’s foot, a section should be made with thick portions (ghanāṃśakaiḥ). It is seen with one, or likewise with two, or even with three [sections]. Therefore, its movement proceeds from the top of the pillar; thus, the tip of the flame is below within the support. In the middle, it should never be joined with the diameter of the pillar. Whether on the right or on the left, that which extends to the very top of the pillar—the middle of the joint should be applied there; in this way, it becomes the ground of all prosperities.

Alternatively, when the width of the base (pādaviṣkambha) is divided into four parts, one may likewise extend [the pillar] by one part, two parts, or three parts. Those learned in the Śruti scriptures know that the tip of the inserted joint (ādheyaka) should be placed at the junction (sandhi). Even when piercing the joints of one another, one should especially avoid piercing the pegs (kīla), as well as a symmetrical joint (samasandhi), for these bring death to the human dwelling. One should join the peg to the base-width at one part, or at the ninth part, while its thickness (bahala) should be half of that.

The *potikā* (pedestal) should be known to be of three kinds according to its names: the *tridaṇḍā*, the *caturdaṇḍā*, and the *pañcadaṇḍā*, in that order. Furthermore, in reverse order, they are the *mahārṇavī*, the *citrī*, and the *patrī*. It should be made with an *oṃ* [shape] from the width, joined with either a quarter or a half [of the total height]. Chapter Eight. For all those who are reclining, the base is said to be the support. The foremost of materials is to be placed upon it, and it is fashioned at the joint.

The distinction between long and wide dimensions arises from the relative strength [of the measurements]. Wherever a certain number of cubits may exist, and wherever a particular *yoni* (source-base) occurs, that shall possess the status of the principal member (*aṅgin*), as well as the status of being the strongest and the support. Other members belonging to it, as well as those to be supported, should be arranged according to their respective strengths. For all [the parts], the tips are conceived as facing north and east; one should join root with root, and one should not join tip with tip.

The junction of the two roots with the two tips leads to the destruction of the site; however, this does not cause any defect when applied to the width, length, or corners. (53) One should place the tip against the northeast (Īśāna), the root against the southeast (Pāvaka), the root against the southwest (Nirṛti), and the root against the northwest (Māruta). Then, one should form the rear portion as a square at the joints where they meet. Some wise men say that one should leave out a quarter, a third, or half [of the space]. (54–55) One who knows the measures of size, height, and proportion should make the thickness equal to half the width.

Generally, the *cūlikā* (finial) and other such elements are prescribed by Vyāsa himself. However, in some cases, a small pinnacle (*kṣudravājana*) is desired for the *rūpottara*. Likewise, the middle section of the *aṅghri* (pedestal/base) is intended for the sake of ornamentation. In the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*), these five—[the aforementioned] as well as the *asūra* fixed with stone and walls joined with lime—are seen as censurable when found in a human dwelling. Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Construction of Halls," in the Science of Architecture. Now begins the ninth chapter.

Now I shall describe, in brief and according to the rules, the measurement of the pedestal (*pāda*); this is proclaimed as being situated between the two northern sandals (*upānaha*). From three finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) onwards, it should be increased by one finger-breadth at each subsequent step; one should have it constructed for a mortal’s residence according to its beauty and suitability. One-third of that [height] is the first part; the pedestal is desired to be made with two parts, or with one part out of four, or with one part out of five. The *masūraka* (the base slab) should be twenty-three parts, seven parts, or eight parts [of the whole].

Twenty-four parts of seven, nineteen parts of ten, thirteen parts of four, eighteen parts of five, one part of six, and a quarter of fifteen; thirty-three parts of ten, and thirty parts of eight—thus one should fashion the measurements of the initial sections according to their application. The wise should know the names and forms of these according to their respective proportions. A skillful artisan should make the height of the couch (mañcaka) into nine parts.

One should know that the *pādukā* (pedestal) is one part and the *kuṭṭima* (flooring) is seven parts; when the height is divided into twelve parts, they know the *pādukā* to be two parts. (8) The height of the *kuṭṭima* is seven parts, and the *pratī* (plinth) is said to be three parts; this is known as the "Trivarga" (the triad), so some wise ones understand it. (9) This is known by the name *pratimañcaka*, and the wise know it to be common for all men; even when the height is made of five parts, the *pādukā* shall be one part. (10)

One should fashion its *jagati* as two parts and its neck (*kaṇṭha*) as one part. The height of the *pratī* should be one part; by name, that is the *galamañcaka*. Its height should be made twelve parts, and one part shall be its *pādukā*. One should know the *kuṭṭima* to be six parts and the neck (*gala*) to be five parts. One should know its *prastara* to be one part, and its *galamañca* is thus described. When the height is made of equal parts, the *pādukā* shall be three parts.

The world [of the temple] consists of six parts; the *kumuda* (fillet) occupies one part for its appearance. The *paṭṭikā* (band) shall be made with one part, and the *antarī* (inner recess) with two parts. Each subsequent band is likewise one part, while the *pratirucaka* (counter-fillet) is said to be two parts; this is called the *pādabandha* (foot-binding), which bestows auspiciousness upon all castes. I shall now describe the ornamentation of the *kumuda* according to its visible parts: the lower band is one part, and the middle part is three parts.

In the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*), the upper frieze (*ūrdhvapaṭṭa*) and the formation of the octagon by means of two [parts] should be made; thus the height of the pedestal (*vedikā*) shall be formed by dividing it into six parts. One part shall be for each panel (*pratipaṭṭa*), and by two parts the inner recess (*antarī*) shall be formed. That upper frieze shall be one part, and the inner recess shall be adorned with flowers. This is declared to be the general form of the pedestal for paved floors (*kuṭṭima*). Furthermore, when the height of the *pratikrama* is divided into twenty-four parts: [the proportions follow].

One should know that the *pādukā* (base) is three parts; the *jagati* (plinth) shall be one-eighth [of the total height]. The *kairava* (neck) shall be seven parts, and the *prati* (fillet) is said to be six parts. Thus, when the height of the *prati* is divided into ten parts, the *kairava* shall be three parts and its *kaṇṭhapaṭṭikā* (neck-band) two parts. The *antarī* (inner recess) shall be three parts, and the *vājana* (coping) is desired to be two parts. It is adorned with the characteristic marks of lions, serpents, lordly elephants, and so forth.

Having divided the altar-base (vedikā) into six equal parts, one part shall constitute each plank (paṭṭa), and with two parts there shall be an intermediate space (antarī). One part shall be for the upper molding (ūrdhvavājana), and one part shall be for its plank (tatpaṭṭikā). The upper plank (ūrdhvapaṭṭa) shall likewise be one part, and the intermediate space (antarī) shall be adorned with flowers. The base (janman) shall be two parts, the shank (jaṅghā) eight parts, its plank (tatpaṭṭikā) one part, and the neck (gala) two parts. Above that, the upper molding (ūrdhvapra) shall be one part, and the neck (gala) and the seat (añcaka) shall be three parts each.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Measurement of the Foot," in the Science of Architecture (*Vāstuvidyā*). Now begins the tenth chapter. Next, we shall briefly describe the characteristics of the *lupās* (architraves). Their width (*tāra*) is declared to be in proportion to the [width of the] lintel (*uttara*). It may be equal to that, or less by one-quarter, or less by one-eighth or more; or it may be greater by one-quarter, or even greater by three-eighths. Or it may be half of the width and so forth. Thus is the measurement of the breadth proclaimed.

Beginning from one and a half *aṅgulas* up to twelve *aṅgulas*, the thickness of the *lupās* (wooden beams) should be increased by one part (*aṃśa*) and their length by one barleycorn (*yava*). A wise man should fashion them as square as the width of the base structure. He should also arrange the lines for the *lupās* reaching to the midpoint of the *tārā* (the transverse beam). The width of the *tārā* is declared to be measured from its corner to the edge of the *koṭi* (the vertical beam). A wise man should multiply the height of the bamboo rafters, ending at the top of the *uttara* (the upper timber), by its own [unit]. The lengths of the positions of the *lupās* are determined by the hanging of the bamboo rafters.

In the science of architecture (vāstuvidyā), having multiplied each [measurement] by its own quality-factor (guṇa) and added them together for the separate construction of the beams (vaṃśa), that root-measure is indeed the measurement of the lintels (lupā); one should calculate it thus everywhere. (7) One should also calculate there by means of that which is the vertical support from the northern end; such is the measurement of all the lintels proclaimed by the wise. (8) Having multiplied half the width (tārā) by the quality-factor and added the height of the beam (vaṃśa), whatever the desired interval between the lintels may be, measured from the central peg (kīla) of the pinnacle (cūlikā)—(9)

Having multiplied that by ten and added half the height of the stars (tārārdhoccakṛta), one should determine the length of the desired *lupā* from the desired junction. The *dhvaja-sūtra* (flag-line) should be drawn from the base to the tip on both sides; the interior [measurement] from the line should be made according to the width of the *cūlikā*. The wise [architect] should determine the length of the *lupā* from the northern edge to the end of the *nīvrā*; from the *nīvrā*, he should fashion a circular rim (*valaya*) in five parts. When the canopy (*vitāna*) is divided into three parts, it should be constructed at the two joints.

The wise one should divide the measurement of the upper shaft (vaṃśa) into five parts. The space between the lower rim (valaya) and the upper rim should be made equal to two parts (netra). Alternatively, when divided by seven (śaila), the space above should be made equal to three parts (rāma). The space between the lower and upper rims is two parts; the space between the two rims is also [two parts], and the space above should be made equal to three parts. As for the positions of the lower rim (valaya): one should draw a square using the width of the *lupā* as the side length; from the width of the *prakṛti*, the width of the elongated triangle (āyatāśra) shall then arise.

16 || The thread reaching its edge is called the *vitāna* (diagonal); the thread extending across it, the wise know as the *lambasūtra* (plumb line). 17 || From the *lambasūtra*, the movement of that circle is now described; its progression to the extremity at half the thickness (*baha*) is proclaimed everywhere. 18 || Wherever the heads of the *lupās* are seen at half the diameter, a row is constructed for that many [units] even beyond half the thickness of the *lupās*. 19 ||

That space which lies between the *lamba* (vertical line) and the upper limit (*upakoṭi*) is declared to be its path of movement; one should determine it similarly in other cases as well. (20) Even within the portion of the *prakṛti* of the *lupās*, internal movement is said to occur; however, in the portion of the *koṭi*, the movement extends outward from the *lamba*-line. (21) One should fashion a square aperture according to the measurement of the ring (*valaya*); generally, the ring is stated by the wise to be fourteen *yavas* in size. (22)

In this case, the thickness should be made three finger-breadths, or two finger-breadths, or one and a half finger-breadths, according to what is beautiful and appropriate. A wise man should fashion a square according to the measurement of the ring; here, he should drop the *lupā*-threads for those [sections] reaching half the *tārā*. In the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*), as far as the length of the *lupā*-threads extends, so should the length of the hollows (*suṣira*) be; the hollows of the various modifications (*vikṛti*) shall thus be of rectangular shape.
