The length of this hollow space is indeed neither upwards, nor downwards, nor across; rather, it is where the connection with the *lupā* beams occurs on the northern side. (26) In that place as well, one should likewise construct the hanging lines and the canopy. When the *cūlikā* spires are joined to the *lupā* beams, one should drop horizontal lines. (27) From the hanging lines of the *lupā* beams, even when the *cūlikā* moves horizontally, its movement is prescribed just as that of a circle is traditionally taught. (28) Indeed, the joining of the *lupā* beams on the northern side is half a *pāṇi* [in measure].

The deceptive jointing by means of *lupās* is known as the "joint of the bamboo node" (*veṇuparvābhidha*). Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the *Lupā*," in the Science of Architecture (*Vāstuvidyā*). Now begins the eleventh chapter. Alternatively, for the sake of achieving brevity in practice for those of dull intellect, one should draw [the plan] upon a flat board free from depressions and elevations. (1) A wise man should draw half the width of the house according to the desired measurement; however, the height of the rafters (*vaṃśa*) is generally remembered as being half the width of the two halls (*śālārya*). (2)

The wise have generally stated that the downward slope (*nīvalamba*) is half a quarter (one-eighth) [of the total length]. Having divided the length of the quarter by nine, seven, five, and two, the downward slope of the *nīva* is respectively one-fourth, three-fifths, two-sevenths, and one-eighth. One should mentally determine and draw the width of the northern part. Furthermore, one should draw an upward line from the midpoint of the star-marking (*tārārdha*) extending for two parts. Then, one should draw a cord passing through the corners of those two, extending from the bamboo-frame (*vaṃśa*) to the end of the *nīva*.

One should arrange the various divisions of the rows within the space between the two arms; starting from the *vaṃśa* line up to the *nīvrā*, one should do so sequentially for each row. (6) In the center of every row, one should draw the guiding lines (*sūtra*). Having measured the length of that which lies closest to the vertical line (*lambasūtra*) of the *kūṭa*, and having fixed that measurement on the north side, one should then draw a diagonal line (*karṇasūtra*) at its end. (7–8) That which lies closest to the secondary line (*upasūtra*) of the vertical line—

9–11. Having established that same measurement as before, one should draw a diagonal line (karṇa) toward the north using a plumb-line and other tools. At its end, one should again draw another [line], and then yet another. They know that form which lies along the diagonal between the tips of the peak and the north to be the *prakṛti*. That line which was previously drawn as the diagonal between the two arms of that measurement is called the *koṭi* by those learned in the science of architecture (*śilpaśāstra*). In the science of building sites (*vāstuvidyā*), those lines situated within that interval are known as the *upakoṭi* and so forth.

On the lower part of the northern side, one should draw two lines (12). These should be equal to the width of the *prakṛti* for the sake of establishing the width of the *vikṛti*. Starting from the perpendicular line (*lamba-sūtra*) and reaching the diagonal line (*karṇa-sūtra*), whatever is the length of the lines situated between the perpendicular and the diagonal, those widths are known as the *lupās* (13–14). One should draw two lines from the corner at the beginning of the diagonal line; the distance between those two lines there is desired to be four finger-breadths (15).

Whichever of the lines extending from the tip of the ear and so forth is longer, that serves as the means for determining the length of those situated between them. (16) If the distance from the center to the edge is half a cubit (*hasta*), and the *lupā* measures six *mānas*, it should be understood by the wise through the rule of three (*trairāśika*), whether it be less or more. (17) One should draw two lines somewhere above the northern [point]; the thickness of the circle should be equal, and the interval between those two [lines] should likewise be equal. (18) On both sides, separately, [one should mark] the lines starting from the plumb line (*lamba*) up to the ear-line.

The sūtras for the *lupās* have indeed been declared to be half as many as those for the *sūtras*. Since the intersection of the ear-sūtra occurs at the sūtra of the circle (*valaya*), one should draw a horizontal line starting from there and ending at the edge of the side-sūtra. One should draw in exactly the same manner even upon the sūtras situated within that. There is no difference in the vertical sūtra between the horizontal and the circular sūtras; rather, throughout the circle, the measurement of the movement is the horizontal interval. However, the interval that exists between two sūtras drawn across the half-circle—

Whatever length belongs to the *lupas* situated within that interval is indeed proclaimed here as the measurement of the hollow’s depth (23). One should place a single thread between the two threads of the half-width; from the lower thread to the middle thread, according to the measurement of the width of the *cūlikā* (24). Wise men know that thread in the treatises on architecture as the *dhvajasūtra*. The portion below the *dhvajasūtra* is intended to be the interior of the banner (25). From the corner up to the end of the diagonal thread (*koṭisūtra*), there are separate threads on both sides.

Each of the *lupās* is said to have another [measurement] similar to that of Vyāsa. One should first lay out the lines for the *sūtras* and then determine the lines for the *dhvajas*. Whatever measurements exist between the two inner *dhvajas*, the wise know those to be the measurements for the hanging threads of the canopy (*vitāna*). Experts in all crafts should draw the *dhvaja-sūtra* along the sides of the *lupā* planks using a thread smeared with ink. One should then apply the measurements starting from the *dhvaja-sūtra* for both the canopy and the hanging [elements].

Wherever the conjunctions of the *māna* (measure) and *udara* (belly) arise in the ten [sections], there two *bindus* (points) are to be established, and one should place them in the root-conjunction (*mūlayoga*). (30) By means of the conjunction of the banner (*dhvaja*) situated within the womb of the *vidyā*, one should draw a line to the end of the back. That same line should go transversely, and likewise on the other side as well. (31) One should draw [the lines] in this manner in all the previously mentioned locations. The movement according to the measure of the path is proclaimed to be as before. (32) The length is stated by the aforementioned measure, and the width by the measure of the circle (*valaya*).

One who is expert in the scriptures should thus create the hollow of the ring. All the *lupās* (wooden beams) are proclaimed to have their roots downward and their tips upward. The width of the tail-end (*puccha*) is declared to be increased by one part out of its own ocean-parts (four parts). A single thread for the canopy (*vitānaka*) should be made at the base of the *lupā*; there, one should cut with an axe and afterwards perform the planing. One should draw a line across the belly at the base of the *lupā* from the canopy; that length is proclaimed to be equal to the thickness of the *lupā*.

36 || One should also draw its horizontal line like a canopy; that depression must be corrected according to the measure of the two [lines]. 37 || Having cut it in that manner, it should be discarded as far as the ring hangs down; likewise between the two rings, and also between the upper rings. 38 || The fragment at the edge of the ring is recorded as being threefold on the upper side; one should make it above as before, and the depression likewise. 39 || Chapter Eleven.

From the edge of the bamboo frame to the end of the canopy, a depression is desired for the circular rim. At the inner front of the canopy, one should draw a thread facing upwards. Above that thread, the contraction of the width is to be omitted; that which extends outside the banner should be discarded, so that it takes the form of a drawn bow. The depression at the belly of all [the banners] is likewise proclaimed to be exactly like that. Others say this very thing has the appearance of a half-moon; likewise, it should have the shape of a tail, similar to an upturned bow.

The depression at the end of the *nīvrā* (the curved beam) should be fashioned like the back of the calf; above that, it should be shaped like a bow, and one should never fashion it otherwise. The space between the *lupā*s (the small beams) at the position of the *nīvrā* should be one *kara* (hand-span) in measure. This has generally been stated by the wise, perhaps with a slight variation of less or more. The *lupā*s should be made in pairs along the middle of the length and the width. For all the *lupā*s, the thickness of the *khaṇḍī* (the joint or section) is prescribed as being up to seven *aṅgulas* everywhere, according to half the measure of their respective widths.

It should be eight *aṅgulas* and three *aṅgulas*, combined with five *yavas*. Thus, by increasing the *aṅgula* and above that by increasing the *yava*, [the dimensions are determined]. Alternatively, for the sake of facilitating the practice of those of dull intellect, I shall again state the characteristics in brief according to another method. Just as it is in the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*) regarding the center of the desired fruit, so one should draw it upon the ground; its magnitude is declared to be equal to the measurement of the house.

Having placed a wooden board nearby according to one’s own respective sūtra, one should then draw the canopy (vitāna) with a thread that has reached the circular frame. One should drop vertical threads through the middle of the transverse lines of the canopy. A cubit (kiṣku) consists of twenty-four barley-corns (yava), and therein the hand (kara) is itself [the unit]; since it is the measure and the means of accomplishment, from this distinction arises here. All the remaining work of craftsmanship should be performed as before.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Construction of the *Lūpā*," in the Science of Architecture (*Vāstuvidyā*). Now begins the twelfth chapter. Furthermore, when the northern *viṣkambha* (width) is divided into ten parts, the *nīvrapaṭṭī* (the base-course band) shall consist of eight parts, or else four and a half, or seven. Its thickness (*bāhalya*) shall be one-third of that, and its width (*vyāsa*) shall be one-eighth. On the upper course (*ūrdhvapaṭṭa*), it shall be one-third, or in the middle, it shall be one-fourth. Then, when [the width] is divided into five parts, the small *vājana* (projection) shall be one part.

In the Vyāsa [measurement], the portion for the horse (aśvyaṃśa) is said to be one-third of the thickness (ghana). From the width, one-third is the measurement for the corner-beams (karṇa) and the canopy (nīvavitāna); it may also be two-fifths, two-sevenths, or three-sevenths. "Salutations to you, the Blessed One, Pavana (the Wind), of immeasurable power; O Dispeller of Waters, protect this abode of the moving and the unmoving! Having bathed, anointed himself with unguents, and dressed in new garments, one of pure intellect, having thus addressed the Sadāgati (Wind), should fasten the roof-laths (lupā) with iron pins.

Now I shall briefly describe the excellent *dhūlikāroha* rite. One should construct a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) to the northwest of the temple, in proportion to its size. (7) Having constructed a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) there according to the prescribed measurements, and having brought forth the sacred fire (*agni-praṇayana*), one should perform the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) according to rule and thereafter perform the oblation (*homa*). (8) For three days and nights, one should offer clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*) with the mantra of the Mountain-Weapon (*parvatāstra*). Then, on the fourth day, one should offer fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter, and so forth, in due order. (9) Thereafter, one should offer one thousand and eight oblations for each item.

Having fed the best of the twice-born with milk-rice (pāyasa), various kinds of foods, and other delicacies, he should satisfy twenty-four of them with ornaments and other gifts. Then, having given them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) and likewise completed the fire-oblation (homa), he should wash those cloth strips with pure water, coconut water, and milk, together with those very same eminent brahmins, and place them well-positioned in the four directions.

Having sprinkled [the site] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should sprinkle it with the residual clarified butter (*sampātājya*). Then, for the sake of the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*), the preceptor should consecrate (*abhimantrayet*) that which has been purified here and there. Having performed this for the vomiting, the falling, and the drinking [of the offerings], the best of teachers, standing facing the temple together with those chief architects, should say: "Salutations to you, the Blessed One, the Wind, the life-force of all beings! May he be pleased with the dust-removal performed by us. Having thus propitiated him in the four directions according to the rule of circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*), then—

Permitted by the preceptor and by those most excellent of the twice-born, the master builder (sthapati), together with the artisans, having first performed prostrations and with palms joined in reverence, should then petition the Lord of the Guardians of the Quarters (dikpāleśa) as follows: "Salutations to the lotus-feet of the gods on earth; salutations to the God who is both moving and unmoving. Since the protective cloth (nītrapaṭṭa) has thus been prepared, let him grant that which is to be given for the purpose of blocking the dust. Then the master builder, along with the artisans, should perform that [rite] in due order.

Having placed [the materials] at the ends of the cords with great sound of musical instruments, one should first bow to Pavana (the Wind), who is ever-moving, and then to the Guru Gaṇeśa and the deities of the directions. Having performed the worship according to the rules and completed it, one should pray to him and drive in the sacrificial pegs. "Salutation to you, the Blessed One, the Great-Souled Māruta. O Lord, grant me your grace so that the dust may be restrained! || 211 ||

The wise have stated that the width of the wooden plank (paṭṭikā) should be eight barley-corns (yava); experts in the craft declare its thickness to be nine barley-corns. The distance between them is said to be one-quarter less than the thickness. I shall now describe the measurement of the bamboo (vaṃśa) according to the rules: the height of the bamboo is desired to be half or three-quarters of [the total height]; those learned in the scriptures know that its width should be equal to its height.

The *paridhi* (circumference) of all those *vikṛtilupas* is considered by experts in the treatises on architecture (*śilpaśāstra*) to be exactly equal to the total thickness of the *kūṭa*. As many as there are *vikṛtilupas*, so many should be the *aśris* (facets) of the *kūṭa*; or rather, the wise man, skilled in carving, should have it made entirely circular. One should fashion the base of the *kūṭa* at the bottom like a *dhurdhūra* flower bud, with a length exceeding half the width, and likewise with an eye (*netra*) measuring three-quarters of an *akṣa*.

One should fashion a fillet (*paṭṭa*) for the dome (*kūṭa*) equal in width to the *lupā*, the canopy, and the *tāra*. The fillet above should not be like the upper [part]; indeed, below it is solid and above it is hollow. (283) The width of the covering (*apidhāna*) is declared to be half the height of the *tāla*, or a quarter, or even three-quarters; that which faces downwards is thus described. (293) In the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*), the thickness should be equal to the [unit of] birth, or a quarter less, or even one and a half. This is declared to be the covering for the head-region of the person who is the house. (303)

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Prevention of Dust," in the Science of Architecture (*Vāstuvidyā*). Now begins the thirteenth chapter. Next, one should again construct a sloping surface with three strips (*paṭṭikā*), measuring one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) and one cubit (*kara*) respectively, and likewise making it firm and triangular. Having constructed a well (*bāpī*) and filled it with water, one should place two stakes (*śaṅku*) in it. Upon the tops of these two stakes—which are raised to a height equal to the water—one should place two wooden blocks (*pada*). This forms the upper triangle of the triangular structure, with its vertical edge firmly suspended.

One should mark that point on the lower plank of the measuring instrument (yaṃtra) which it touches and then draw a line therefrom. By means of that, the instrument becomes precise; through it, one should determine the low and high points. Where the cord moves vertically, that is the low point, and the other is the high point. When the end of the plank meets the vertical cord, that is the level ground. One should employ a pedestal (upapīṭha) beneath the base (adhiṣṭhāna) for the sake of protection, for height, and for beauty; so they declare.

It should be equal [to the base], or three-quarters, or five parts out of six; or with a quarter added, or half-added, or one-and-a-quarter times [the base]; or indeed twice the height of the *adhiṣṭhāna* (plinth) should be made here. The projection (*niṣkrama*) of its first member, the *pādukā*, is prescribed as one cubit in measure, or less by a quarter, or one cubit, or with a quarter added. It may be one-and-a-quarter cubits, or two cubits; the *upapīṭha* (sub-base) should be constructed according to the methods prescribed for couches and the like.

The outer portion of the *upapīṭha* is declared to be the courtyard (*aṅgaṇa*). In its northeastern quarter, a water-channel should be constructed facing north. Having divided the length of the courtyard into eight parts by a unit (*pada*) slightly less than the width, one should leave aside one *pavaya* in the north and discard one *pada* in the east. On another *pada*, the wise should construct a stone-paved floor (*mahikā-kuṭṭima*), joined with the *upapīṭha* and other elements, square in shape, and possessing the "flag-source" (*dhvajayoni*) configuration. Its height should be equal to its width, or three-quarters of it, as is appropriate.

It should be constructed with beds and other furnishings in accordance with the dimensions of the house and its constituent parts. Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the layout for all dwellings; when an auspicious moment for building houses has arrived, the master builder himself—having bathed according to the rules for laying the foundation (vāstu), having put on two smooth, new garments, and being adorned with all ornaments such as upper cloths and ointments—should worship Gaṇādhīśa and bestow wealth upon the Brahmins.

For the sake of the initial rite, he—standing facing the east accompanied by the blessings uttered by the twice-born—should place the sandals there. Having mentally determined the temple from its birth to its covering, he should perform the measurement of the leaf (patramāna) as follows: to the north of the birth [point], he should draw a line eight finger-breadths wide all around, extending toward the various directions. This measurement of the leaf is generally prescribed for the dwellings of men.

Otherwise, it is proclaimed that there is an external womb (bahir-yoni) apart from [the presence of] compassion and the like. Having prepared the surrounding foundation (upāna), one should place the sandals (pāduka) there. The placement of the embryo (garbha-nyāsa) is prescribed on the southern pillar of the door. For a Brāhmaṇa, it is traditionally held that the sandals should be placed upon [the embryo]; for kings, below that; for Vaiśyas, below that; and for those of Śūdra birth, below that. The preceptor (deśika) should then place the Janman mantra upon the head of the Jagatī and so forth.

Having done this, one should place that first limb, the *talipa*, there. (22) I shall describe the acquisition of wood for the characteristics of the treasure-house later; I will not speak of it here for fear of excessive prolixity. (23) A door must be made in all directions for all dwellings. The center of the middle door should coincide with the two threads of the *vāstu* mandala. (24) The secondary doors are joined in a clockwise direction starting from their own source.

The width of the door-jamb should be equal to the height of the lintel (uttara). The door-sockets (yonis) for houses and other structures should be made according to their respective origins. A wise man should divide the space between the lintel (prastara) and the lintel above (uttara) into five parts. One-fourth of the door’s height should be the remaining portion; when this is divided by twelve, the head-measurement (śiraḥ) is seven parts and the ankle (gulpha) is desired to be five parts. The remainder of the height is declared to be the width of the circumference. When the space between the lintel and the lintel above is divided into eight parts...

One should make the length seven parts and the width nine parts; having divided the remaining height by nine, the head (śiras) shall be five parts. The expert in the scriptures should make the measurement of the ankle four parts, or alternatively, he may construct the door with a width of three parts as is appropriate. The temple and its door are prescribed to face south in the southeast (āgneyī); it faces west in the southwest (nairṛtī), and it faces north in the northwest (vāyavī).

One should place that facing east; they should be positioned upon the footstool (pādukā). Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the Door," in the Science of Architecture (Vāstuvidyā). A wise man should construct a pair of door-panels known as the Mother and Daughter. When the width of the door (dvāratāra) is divided into four, five, six, seven, or eight parts, one part shall be the strip for the cord (sūtrapaṭṭi). Its thickness (bahala) may be equal [to its width], or it is proclaimed that the thickness may be half, or even less by a quarter.

The width and length of the doors should be equal, and the rows should be in pairs; these are proclaimed as the "rows" (paṅkti) extending up to the houses for horses and other animals. || 3 || At the front junctions, there should be lotuses numbering from eight (agni) up to sixty-four (aty-aṣṭi); their height should be half a tārā or one-third of it. || 4 || Alternatively, one may make the height half of the thickness (bahaḷa) when the height is divided into ten parts; the upper panel (ūrdhva-paṭṭa) should be one part, and within that, there should be three parts. || 5 ||

It should also be circular, endowed with eight petals and provided with filaments; below that, the base-slab (*adhaḥpaṭṭa*) shall consist of one part, being square and equal in height [to the width]. Two lotuses should be made at the base and the top, variegated and increasing by half [in size]; their petals should be without angles and adorned with strings of pearls. The door-opening should have a width of half the door itself, increased by one-fourth of the slab; it is desired to be joined with its own thickness. And the *putrikā* (ornamental figure) should have a width reduced by half of that slab.

In each of the measurements beginning with *vasu* (eight) and ending with *saṃkṛti* (forty-eight), that [thickness] shall be exactly one [unit]. (9) The thickness of the door-panel (*kavāṭa*) should be according to the measurement of the width of the doorway. The two legs of the frame (*raṅgapāda*) should be made perfectly circular at both their tips and their bases. (10) The base-block (*mūlapāduka*) should have a length equal to its own thickness, or one and a half times; the length of the top-block (*agrapāda*) should be similar to the thickness of the beam (*bhāra*). (11) It may be one and a half times or double [the thickness], according to what is beautiful and as firm as possible. The length of the beam (*bhāra*) is said to be equal to the width (*tāra*) of the two door-panels. (12)

The two tails of the *bhāra* (the central beam) are said to have a length equal to their width. The *bhāratāra* (the central axis of the beam) should be constructed toward the door using the *samādibhiḥ* (the proportions beginning with the *sama*). The thickness (*bahala*) of the *bhāratāra* should be equal, one-quarter less, or half [of its width]. When the *bhāratāra* is divided by four (*abdhisaṃbhakte*), one should drop three lines. Three horizontal lines should also be made between the middle of the door and the two *āprayaḥ* (thresholds). By means of the rotation of a compass whose foot is placed at the junction of the first line, [the circle is drawn].

A broken section (*khaṇḍi*) should be made outside the third thread from the [central] line; in this way, three broken sections should be made, with their base, tip, and middle being recessed. Wherever there is a horizontal line joined to a recessed section, that should be decorated. Indeed, artisans must avoid any angularity located in the middle of a joint. When a circular cavity is to be made, [the measurement is taken] from the two horizontal threads on the outside; the first section shall be at the end of the outer portion of the initial thread.

In the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*), one should apply [the measurement] above the threshold and the door-posts by half a *pāṇi*; furthermore, one should ensure firmness through the piercing of pegs, stakes, and the like. (19) One should thus construct the lower beam (*adhobhāra*) free from any central joint; the first square (*pada*) is to be omitted, and two cavities (*avaṭa*) are to be made in the second. (20) According to the measurement of the stage-pillar (*raṅgapāda*), it should be circular and half-sunken; then, having taken one part out of four parts of the fillet (*paṭṭikā*) from the side, (21)

One should insert the cord of the door-panel (mātṛsaṃjñaka) inside; having led it through separately at the base and the top, making it equal to the thickness [of the panel], one should place a strip of cord in the middle of that at the base, either half [the thickness] or less by a quarter. One should make the strip immovable by piercing it with pegs shaped like lotus buds or resembling flowers, placed in the centers of the lotuses, with their tips pointing upward in the middle. The width of the door-arch (arama) is declared to be one-ninth of the height of the doorway.

The thickness [of the bolt] is known by the best of artisans to be one part out of sixteen, or five, six, or one parts; or it may be half of the width, or equal to it. It is described by the most skilled craftsmen as having a shape that matches the weight below. When its length is divided by four, one part each should be discarded from both ends; having placed two parts in the middle, one should place the bolt-joint at that junction. One should fashion the *kavalī* there according to the measurement of the bolt; they know the length of the bolt to be equal to the width of the door-panel.

It should be one-eighth less than that, or even one-sixteenth; it should be as thick as the *tāra* (the door-jamb). One should make the *tāra* thick, and the two panels (*khaṇḍau*) should be equal in thickness to that. This is declared to be the root-panel (*mūlakhaṇḍa*), which is as long as its own width. The length of the front panel (*agrakhaṇḍī*) should be half or even one-quarter less. The wise have stated that the tail (*puccha*) should have a thickness and length equal to the spokes (*aramā*). Some say there may be a single side-panel (*upaḍāraka*) and a door-leaf (*kavāṭa*). The thickness of the door-leaf should be twice the thickness of the door-jamb (*dvāratāra*).

On the left side of both the base and the top [of the door], there should be two colored lines (raṅgavāda). The length is said to be one bhāra and one fire (three) bhāras; its single section should be like the base and top in terms of the bhāra. A pit and a peg (śaṅku) should be made, and it should be exactly one span (vitasti) in length. One should divide the thickness of the door-panel (kavāṭa), the thickness of the frame (ḍimba), and the width by means of the upper region, and in one of the two positions, by means of the rotation of a compass (karkibhrama) placed in the middle of the width and length of the panel.

One should make a circular pit at the base, depressed by half the height of the painted panel (raṅgapāda). Then it should be made octagonal, or indeed shaped like the back of an elephant. (36) Its depth is declared by those skilled in the craft to be half its width. Its breadth is proclaimed to be three times the thickness of the door-leaf (kavāṭa). (37) Its length is said to be twice that; one should then divide the breadth into three parts. In the middle of those [three], a hole for the bolt (argala) should be made. (38)

In the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*), it may be square or circular as is appropriate. The thickness of the bolt (*behalam*) is said to extend from the side of the pillar to the edge of the door-leaf. Its width and length are prescribed to be equal to that thickness; its tail (*puccham*) is declared to be equal to the thickness or three-quarters of it. It is also described as being either square or circular. Having taken one-third of the thickness, [one should apply it] to its tip and base.

One should make a pit between those [two] spokes; that is called the *taccāra*. Its width and depth should each be one-third of its own thickness. There should be a hollow (*suṣira*) on the inner side of the spoke or on its back. In that hollow, there should be a piercing by a pin (*kīla*), provided it is not obstructed by the bolt (*margala*). Having placed a weight beneath it, or even two stakes (*śaṅku*), one should properly place the mother (*mātṛ*) on the left side within that pit.

One should place the supports for the upper and lower sections with the feet as appropriate; if there is only one [support], it is prescribed to be on the right side, and the *putrikā* (female figurine) on the left. At the southern pillar, there should be a spoke (*ara*) or even a chain (*śṛṅkhalā*); one should properly fix the load and so forth with iron pins (*kīlaka*). Thus ends the fourteenth chapter on the arrangement of doors and spokes in the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*). One may construct a wall that is exceedingly firm using stone, clay, or wood.

Thus, here has been described in detail a corresponding and abundant [method] for the base (talipa) and other parts. (1) One should construct the wall such that its top is reduced by one part out of the total height; the outer portion should be made so that it is level with the inner portion. (2) On an auspicious moment, under a favorable constellation, during the bright fortnight and at a time of rising good fortune, the master builder (sthapati), having bathed and anointed himself, should put on the fivefold ornaments. (3) Having given sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins and having gratified the carpenters with wealth, [he should proceed].

Having worshipped Gaṇeśvara, one should then perform the rite for an auspicious day (puṇyāha). After giving the sacrificial fee (dakṿiṇā) for the auspicious moment, the northern [structure] should be covered with cloths. It should be properly installed against the walls or otherwise fixed within the beams (amiṣu). Then, while touching it again, one should mutter mantras such as the Svasti-sūkta. Having joined it with the northern [components], one should subsequently place the crest (cūlikā) all around. The wise man, having made it firm with wooden pegs (kīla), should join it with balances (tulā).

One should construct the expansion of the *tulās* (balconies) to the north, beginning with a square unit (*sama*) and so forth. One should decorate the *tulās* with a decorative band (*sūtrapaṭṭikā*). Here, pairs of lotuses are prescribed, while the rows are known to be odd in number. In the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*), the height of the *tulā* legs is desired to be equal to the width of the *alinda* (porch). The porch situated between the outer ascending [balcony] and the northern [balcony] is called the middle one. The width of the ascending northern [balcony] is equal to the northern [unit] and so forth.

Its minimum extent, however, is sixty-four finger-breadths and so forth. Scales should indeed be made in pairs; odd-numbered ones are recorded as being for liquids. Above the scale, the upper structure should be constructed, mounted and provided with a pinnacle (*cūlikā*). Bamboo legs should be fashioned, and upon them one should again place bamboo. The two roof-structures (*kūṭau*) should be joined with bamboo, made firm by the piercing of pegs (*kīla*). All the rafters (*lupāḥ*) should be set up and properly fixed with pegs.

Having performed the piercing of the rings and the binding of the rings, one should fashion all the ornaments and so forth like those of a balance-beam; the width [of the beam] should be three times that of the rings, and its thickness should be one-fourth of its width. Having placed the *nīva* (the central block) and the side-boards (*paṭṭikā*), one should then place a pigeon-hole (*pārāvata*) in each of the corners of the *nīva*. For the purpose of covering the joints of the *nīva* and for the protection of the clods of earth, one should again firmly fix it with pegs and piercings at the two *nīvas*.

At an auspicious moment and under a favorable constellation, the wise architect, as before, should raise the covering—which is concealed by a cloth—upward and secure it with stakes (17). Having struck them, he should ensure firmness everywhere at the joints; he should perform the installation of the bolt at an auspicious moment when a favorable planetary rising occurs (18). The wise man should place the upper bolt upon the female figure with its front facing left, and furthermore, he should install the goddess Lakṣmī above it with her face turned upward (19).

Having measured half the length of the bolt from the door-line toward the south, one should place the *ara* there; for another [door], another [measurement] is prescribed. An expert in the scriptures should place that [bolt] in the middle of the door's width, with its tip pointing south and situated below; this is known as the "bolt of the brother" (*bhrātṛ-argala*). Having also placed the *aramā* as before by means of piercing with a peg (*kīla*), and having made it firm according to the rule, one should offer the *vāstu-bali* at night.

Having completed the work on the site there according to the prescribed method, one should further cover the house there with many cloths. Then the patron should duly honor those craftsmen, having given them anointing oils and other comforts as is appropriate after they have bathed. He should give garments, ointments, fragrant flowers, and all kinds of ornaments such as earrings to everyone as is fitting.

Having offered the four kinds of food, even those endowed with the six flavors, one should say, "Let it be given according to one's ability; let the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) be given thereafter. Having thus satisfied them all, he should say to them, "Please accept this house. Then the architect (sthapati), having accepted all that—including the sacrificial fees and so forth—should recite these mantras together with the laborers: "From the falling of rainwater, from the striking of lightning, from fierce winds, and even from the burning of fire..."

By the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*), may this dwelling be protected from thieves and the like, from the assault of enemy armies, and from gods and asuras. (283) May men be free from disease, wealthy, happy, and long-renowned for their glory. May the virtuous king, victorious, protect the entire earth abounding in cattle and crops. (293) Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, the Moon and the Sun, Nandin, Lakṣmī, Vāg-vadhū, Skanda, and Indra...

May the earth, the gods, and the sages bestow upon living beings prosperity, good fortune, health, and enjoyments. (303) May the sky be firm and may the earth be firm; may these mountains be stable. May this entire universe be eternal, and likewise may the king and his royal power be eternal. (313) Brahmā himself is the chief architect, Hari is the patron of the sacrifice, and the Lord Rudra is the preceptor—that which has been accomplished by these three. (323)

That site shall indeed be firm and bestow both seen and unseen fruits. Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Acquisition of a Dwelling," in the Science of Architecture (Vāstuvidyā). Now, I shall briefly describe the characteristics of clay for mortar and plaster: that which is sticky, that called pale-white, and that which is salty are condemned. The fourth type, copper-colored and blooming, is considered suitable for work. [One should avoid soil] containing husks, charcoal, bones, stones, wood, gravel, and clods of earth.

Having removed fine sand and those stones known as *tāmraphulla*, one should throw them into a pit and pour water knee-deep into it. Having stirred it with the feet and agitated it, one should trample those [stones] again and again. Then, for the duration of a month, they should be crushed by men skilled in that work with milk, the sap of the *āgastya* tree, a decoction of *śirīṣa* bark, and water infused with the three myrobalans (*triphalā*). One should properly fashion clods from them; their characteristics are now described.

The *nīvraloṣṭa*, the *ūrdhvaloṣṭa*, the square (*caturaśra*), the *krūraloṣṭaka*, the *hyaśraloṣṭa*, the *kīlaloṣṭa*, the *kṛśāgra* (thin-tipped), the *sthūlāgra* (thick-tipped), the *gartakoṇa* (pit-cornered), the *koṇaloṣṭa*, and likewise the *puṭaloṣṭa*—these are the eleven types of *loṣṭas*. Their dimensions, such as length and so forth, are now described. The width of the *nīvrapaṭī* should be four finger-breadths (*aṅgulas*). This is declared by those learned in the science of *loṣṭas* to be the length of the *nīvraloṣṭa*. One should make its width two finger-breadths and its thickness one-quarter of that span.

The thickness at the top of all [the parts] should be half of that; the head [of each] is like the preceding joint. According to the science of architecture (vāstuvidyā), the height of the upper brick (mūrdhvaloṣṭa) is desired to be twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas); its width is one-third of that, and they know its thickness to be six barley-corns (yavas). The thickness of the corners of the pits called *puṭas* is like that of the lower brick (nītraloṣṭa). Its length should be eight finger-breadths, and now its width is described: the base of the *puṭa* is four finger-breadths, and its tip is one and a half finger-breadths.

The root of the millions of *gartas* (pits) is declared to be one and a half finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). The tip should be four finger-breadths, with a shape like a harsh clod of earth (*krūraloṣṭa*). They know the base of the corner to be eight finger-breadths and the tip to be one and a half finger-breadths. Regarding the five types beginning with *nīpra*, there is a distinction; the three beginning with the *kīla* (peg) have a width equal to half their respective *tārā*. The *krūraloṣṭa* is declared [to have that same measure]. For those with harsh or elongated corners, the length is said to be eight finger-breadths (*vasu*), the width is stated to be two finger-breadths, and the thickness is considered to be three barley-corns (*yava*).

15 || That which has a width equal to half the root-star and a thin tip is proclaimed [as such]; since its root is half the length of the tip-star, it is designated as having a thick tip. 16 || For all [types], the tip is desired to be half the thickness of the root; that which is of uniform thickness throughout and has a rounded top is designated as a *loṣṭa*. 17 || Now, having fashioned a wooden *loṣṭa* endowed with the aforementioned characteristics, with a thickness of one finger-breadth—that is the means for accomplishing all [rites]. 18 || A thread should be applied from root to tip through the middle of the *krūra* [stone].

From the base, one should draw a diagonal line measuring half a *tāra* (unit) to the left. By joining the diagonal at the base with the tip of the center, one should draw [the other lines]; the outer portion is to be discarded, for that constitutes the practice of the cruel deities. Dividing the distance between the two corners by four, one should drop three lines. Having moved from the base by a quarter of a *tāra*, one should drop a diagonal line; by joining the diagonal at the base with the side-tip, one should draw [the figure].

Starting from the tip situated at the side, one should join it with the middle of the horizontal line. Excluding the portion outside the ear-line (karṇasūtra), this shall indeed be the means for establishing the triangle (*aśra*). Having smeared even a wooden board with ashes as a preparatory means, one should spread over it a layer of fine clay of the prescribed thickness. Then, having struck it and made it level, one should place the instrument upon it. Having fixed a joint at its tip with pegs made of bamboo or other materials—

One should cut away the side and the root; this is the rule prescribed for all cases. Having extracted them while they are slightly dried, one should then strike them oneself. One should cause the upper clod and the corner clod to be struck. One should fashion the *koṇapārāvata* and the coverings for the *stūpī*. For those dried in the shade, one should perform the burning as is appropriate. In the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*), having prepared the hearth (*cully*) according to the wind's direction during an auspicious conjunction (*sulagna*) when the moon is not in a blind asterism (*anandharkṣa*).

There, one should heat clods of earth and place them down gradually with intervals between them. [The pit] should be filled without gaps using wood, bundles of straw, and so forth; it should be properly covered on the outside and smeared with clay. Having placed fire at its openings for ten days or even a fortnight, once the fire has been extinguished after the consecration, one should again remove the clods. Alternatively, another method for burning the clods is prescribed: having strewn dry branches of the *ciñcā* tree and others during an auspicious moment.

Having laid down pieces of wood, one should lay down stalks of straw. Having placed clods of earth upon that, one should cover it again with straw. Afterwards, having covered it with straw-masks, and likewise with rice-husks and tufts of grass, one should then sprinkle it with water and set the branch on fire again. When the fire has been extinguished, the wise man, having removed [the ashes], should cover the house; having laid down stalks and clods, he should also lay down bricks shaped like squares.

Thereafter, one should place the sacrificial bricks (yaṣṭi) in this very manner again and again; having placed the harsh clods of earth according to their beauty and according to one’s intelligence (35); having placed the pigeon-shaped brick at the corner, one should place the corner-clods; on both sides, one should place the side-clods and the upper-clods (36); having placed the corner-pits, one should place the *kalā* and other elements as is appropriate; at an auspicious moment and under a favorable asterism, one should place the covering for the stūpa (37); and likewise, the worship of the carpenters should be performed exactly as prescribed for them.

Likewise, in temples and other such structures, [the measurement] may be made with gold and the like; however, the quantity of earth or clods of earth should be understood according to the available materials. Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Earth and Clods," in the Science of Architecture (Vāstuvidyā). The Science of Architecture is completed. May there be auspiciousness!
